title: Make the most of spring asparagus with these recipes
text:
It's the perfect time to be cooking asparagus.

Blossoms and hay fever concerns aside, spring is really about asparagus season. A time for asparagus lovers to rejoice and an annual opportunity for sceptics to get onside.

From one-pot pasta to a crunchy green salad, these four recipes will help you embrace those delicious green spears while they are affordable.

One-pot pasta is a speedy weeknight dinner with hardly any washing up. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

With a cooking time of just 15 minutes and minimal prep, this one-pot pasta recipe from Heidi Sze combines about two bunches of asparagus and a lot of staple ingredients.

Lemon and capers will help brighten the dish and either tinned or cooked salmon fillet could be substituted for the tuna, she says.

You can make this vegetarian galette ahead of time and keep it in the fridge for up to three days. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

Hetty Lui McKinnon's galette recipe is an unfussy and adaptable vehicle for your favourite spring vegetables.

The corn could be replaced with fresh peas, podded broad beans, green beans, thinly shaved fennel, broccoli, or crunchy sugar snap or snow peas, Hetty says.

And it can be enjoyed either warm or at room temperature, making any leftovers a potentially perfect work lunch candidate.

Hetty Lui McKinnon's hearty sauce transforms a salad into a main meal. (ABC Everyday: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

Another recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon, who says this salad is "high on texture and assertive with spring vibes".

If you're not familiar with sauce gribiche, it brings together vinegar, cornichons, capers, mustard and chopped hard-boiled eggs.

"The iconic French sauce is part chunky vinaigrette, part punchy mayonnaise," according to Hetty.

This rich and silky quiche will feed 8-10 people. (ABC News: Thalia Ho)

This quiche recipe from Thalia Ho is simple to assemble and includes beginner-friendly pastry.

Asparagus, lemon and goats' cheese is a tried and tested flavour combination, but Thalia says "you can play around with the filling, depending on taste, craving and what's available".

title: Australia's Rugby League World Cup squad is a sign of the changing times
text:
The depths of Australia's star power means the Kangaroos will always name squads oozing with class and Kevin Walters's combination for this year's World Cup is no exception.

It's a side with major success stories, young and old and in-between.

James Tedesco's return three years after his last Test caps the 33-year old's resurrection and after he ran the ball to hell and back in the grand final to win the Clive Churchill Medal, there can be no doubt that, at an age where many players best days are only just a memory, he is once again the best fullback in the world.

Walker among six Kangaroos debutants The grand final sides feature in the Kangaroos squad for the Rugby League World Cup, with James Tedesco back in and Sydney's Sam Walker and Newcastle's Bradman Best among six debutants.

The inclusion of Dolphins flyer Jack Bostock, who will almost certainly see a Test debut in the World Cup opener given the side's shortage of wingers, heralds the start of a new generation wearing green and gold.

At 26, David Fifita is no longer a youngster in rugby league terms but his looming Australian debut is both a long time coming and well-earned following his strong finish to the year with Souths.

The one-time prodigy has longed seemed a player of limitless possibilities but only now, eight years after his NRL debut and three years since he last played for Queensland, will he get the chance to be a Kangaroo.

But the Australian squad also reveals the new truths about representative football, that the disconnect between State and Origin and Test matches is wider than ever before and may never be stitched back together again.

The disconnect between Origin and Test football has never been wider. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

It's a process that began with Origin's gradual but unmistakeable rise past Test football as rugby league's biggest stage then continued when a host of players chose to represent Pasifika nations over Australia while retaining their Origin eligibility.

The final change came earlier this year when the NRL allowed players to represent New Zealand or England and still being available for Origin selection.

Both of those eligibility changes reflect the changing face of rugby league and the people who play it and the game is better for them.

But it does require a reset of over a century's worth of thinking that interstate football is the pathway to national selection.

This has not been true for some years now, but there's a reason old habits have a hard time dying.

And while Australia will never be hard up for talent, some of the more eyebrow-raising picks prove this old adage is as antiquated as Kangaroo tours that travel to England by boat.

Robert Toia would have been a walk-up start for Australia but has chosen Tonga. (Getty Images: Izhar Khan)

Not one of the Queensland outside backs is in the side at all. Kalyn Ponga, Robert Toia, Jojo Fifita, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all would be, but they're playing for other nations while Selwyn Cobbo is injured.

That's how we end up with Brisbane's Kotoni Staggs, a fine centre who had a tough year, making the side despite being dropped by New South Wales for the Origin decider after a horror night in Game II at the MCG.

Latrell Mitchell missed the entire series through injury and has only started one match in the past five months but he's made it, while Tom Trbojevic is a likely starter on one wing despite not having played rep football for two years and not playing a match on the flank since 2018.

Tom Trbojevic will play his first Test match in two years. (AAP: Darren England)

Likewise of the 12 men who played in the forwards for New South Wales, only Blayke Brailey, Isaah Yeo, Liam Martin and Cameron Murray have made the squad.

Hudson Young and Payne Haas are both out with injury, but Haumole Olakau'atu and Addin Fonua-Blake will both line up for Tonga while Victor Radley is with England.

So Reuben Cotter makes the squad despite an underwhelming season with the Cowboys and a lacklustre series for Queensland.

His selection over Dolphins hardman Max Plath, who does a similar job with similar attributes whilst offering the same versatility and is coming off a far superior season for club and state, is perhaps the hardest pick to understand.

How Plath became Queensland's newest Origin hero The players who fill the spaces in between the stars are the secret to Queensland's Origin dominance and in Max Plath the Maroons have found yet another player who knows just how to do it.

Plath, along with Newcastle's Fletcher Sharpe and South Sydney's Tallis Duncan can count himself most aggrieved at missing out but it's hard to take up too much issue with Walters's squad, even if it's short of wingers.

This is the hand the Australian coach has been dealt for his final tournament before he departs to take over Super League side St Helens.

The eligibility changes and the fact that Test football misses out on players who pick up injuries during club seasons that are getting longer and longer all the time means sometimes his options are a bit more limited than he would have liked.

Australia are still the pick to win the World Cup and will be warm favourites in every game they play, beginning with their tournament opener against New Zealand next Thursday night in Sydney.

Walters is attempting to solve a puzzle no other Kangaroos coach has ever had to face and there is no one-size-fits-all philosophy in the battle between fitness, function and form when it comes to selecting a player.

But when numbers are scarce, and for the Kangaroos they're a lot shorter than they used to be, the first two are more important than the last.

title: NBL owner pays state $577 a week to rent stadium
text:
The Tasmanian government has effectively been leasing out a stadium to property developer and NBL owner Larry Kestelman for less than it would cost to rent most houses in the area, a parliamentary report has found.

The Public Accounts Committee found the proposed sale of Wilkinsons Point, home to the Derwent Entertainment Centre, to Mr Kestelman has exposed "serious and longstanding failures" in the management of a public asset and negotiations should be paused until some of its recommendations are implemented.

The Derwent Entertainment Centre, also known as MyState Bank Arena. (ABC News: Scott Ross)

The report into the sale of Wilkinson's Point found that despite six years of negotiations between the Tasmanian government and Mr Kestelman's LK Group, there is no binding sale, no business case and no agreed master plan.

It also found that the LK Group was effectively leasing the Derwent Entertainment Centre (DEC) for less than $30,000 a year.

"Larry Kestelman is a billionaire," Shadow Treasurer Dean Winter said.

" He has already sold the JackJumpers for a reported $35 million, while his company, a separate entity, is now leasing MyState Bank Arena for less than a family pays in rent for a family home in Glenorchy. "

The base rate rent for the DEC is $200,000 a year, adjusted for CPI.

But the Tasmanian government pays the LK Group $175,000, meaning Tasmania makes less than $30,000 a year, or approximately $577 a week.

Larry Kestelman and Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff at a JackJumpers game in 2022. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The report and Mr Winter accused the government of "overstating the revenue and failing to disclose the hiring fee" during the committee process.

"The $175,000 annual subsidy was completely hidden from the Parliamentary Public Works Committee during its 2020 review," Mr Winter said.

" In the hearing, the government overstated revenues. They have never disclosed the $175,000 annual payment back to Kestelman's company. "

The committee said the agreement did allow for LK Group to pay a percentage rent subject to the performance of the DEC, but none had been paid.

The Tasmania JackJumpers celebrate their 2024 NBL Championship win at the DEC. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The committee found that the proposal to sell the land to Mr Kestelman began through Glenorchy City Council, before the state government took over when it acquired the DEC and the land surrounding it in 2020.

Since that time, the Tasmanian government has been working exclusively with the LK Group to sell the land with a price tag of about $6 million.

In February 2025, Premier Jeremy Rockliff announced that the government had agreed to sell the Crown land at Wilkinsons Point to the LK Group "at a value determined by the valuer-general to enable the development" of:

A multi-use retail precinct,

A family resort; and,

A hotel complex.

A report released later that year by the auditor-general found "significant shortcomings in advice and process" and a lack of a government business case to support the policy.

Then in an incoming government brief provided to Business and Industry Minister Felix Ellis following July's state election, the Department of State Growth warned that activating the site could cost taxpayers $100 million.

The departmental brief also detailed that there was "no certainty of development or contribution to costs from LK Group".

"The department's current recommendation is to cease negotiations on sale of land and consider offering the surplus land to open market," the note said.

The committee found a key area of disagreement was how much the car park would cost and who should pay for it.

The department estimated it would cost $100 million, while LK Group thought it would be about half that. It is unclear whether this has been resolved.

In April Mr Kestelman told the committee negotiations were suspended, in part due to the car park, and he was prepared to walk away if necessary.

Talks have since resumed.

In its report, the committee found that no agreement exists on how infrastructure costs will be shared between the government and LK Group, "notwithstanding years of negotiation on this point".

Wilkinsons Point sits on 15 hectares of Crown land, and is the site of the Derwent Entertainment Centre. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Winter said the premier appeared to be "hell-bent on giving Larry Kestelman a good deal, but not at all interested in the interests of Tasmanians".

"Taxpayers face an estimated infrastructure footprint approaching $100 million for car parking, road realignments, and site servicing, with zero agreement on cost-sharing.

"This isn't commercial negotiation; it is complete mismanagement of public assets.

" You do not sell off $100 million in public liabilities for a $6 million headline price without a business case, without market testing and without binding development guarantees."

It recommended that the government pause negotiations until it completes a number of recommendations, including tabling a report that sets out the status of negotiations, any revised development proposal, estimated public costs and progress on the auditor-general's recommendations.

It also recommended that the lease agreement between the government and the LK Group be reviewed.

Asked about the report's findings, government minister Nick Duigan said the government remains committed to the opportunities.

"Wilkinson's Point represents a massive opportunity for Greater Hobart in terms of new housing, activating Dowsing Point," he said.

title: Cowboys and girls dress up for Santa Teresa/Ltyentye Apurte horse races
text:
A crowd cheers as horses gallop past the finishing post, but this is no ordinary race.

On the first weekend in October every year, Indigenous men and women gather for the Santa Teresa/Ltyentye Apurte races, about 70 kilometres south-east of Alice Springs.

In this remote corner of central Australia, helmets are optional, chunky stock saddles replace light saddle pads, and children run barefoot across the red dusty track between races.

The races have been running since about the 1960s. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Behind the rail, spectators swap fascinators for sports caps and reverse their utes up to the track boundary for the best views.

The prize money is enough to cover some extra groceries from town, but jockeys and owners know the event is about more than winning.

Community residents line up around the track boundary to watch the action. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Atyenhenge Atherre Aboriginal Corporation (AAAC) chair Raymond Plamer said the annual amateur race meet had been running since about the 1960s, a time when many of the region's Indigenous people worked as stock workers on cattle stations.

"[It's] very important to us, because we had this race for years for our forefathers," he said.

"We will continue to keep it going."

Raymond Palmer (right) calls the races. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Walkabout Bore horseman Peter Kenny has been coming to the races since the early 90s and said the event was as exciting as ever.

"I love doing this. I love riding horses, watching horses, galloping, getting all the kids and family all together. It's a good thing," he said.

Peter Kenny says the event is a highlight for the community. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Like many who travelled hours over rough, tyre gouging roads to come to the race, Mr Kenny learnt how to handle horses from his father.

"That's what I grew up doing, riding horses and breaking them in all the time," he said.

"I've got my little breeding horses at Walkabout. I breed them up there, handle them, bring them to the races all the time, every year, all these mob."

The remote Indigenous community of Santa Teresa holds a horse race the first weekend of October every year. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Festivities continue after dark

Once the dust settles and the horses have been put away, racegoers flock from the track back to the community.

Later that night, in the dim light of a giant sports hall, hundreds of people from the community, and their visitors, pack in, holding paper plates loaded with potato salad, sausages and steak from the free barbecue outside.

Children dressed in "cowboy clothes" for a best dressed competition. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

It is time for the community dress up evening, the oft-mentioned, highly anticipated evening tradition, where cowboys, cowgirls, cow-women and cow-men put on their best, dressing up and showing off.

Choosing best dressed is a hard job for this year's judge Sidney Mahinya, an occupational therapy student from the city on placement at the local clinic.

"There was all different types of outfits. We had some whip-cracking, we had some chaps, we had really cool boots and amazing hats and even the belts. It was really cool," she said.

Sidney Mahinya has only been in Santa Teresa two weeks, but has already become involved in the community. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Ms Mahinya has been in the community for two weeks and said residents had been welcoming.

"I would definitely like to come back. I think this community is so beautiful and there's so much to offer," she said.

" Being able to be here and learn and just being amongst all the people is just really a wonderful experience. "

title: He was the best forward in the grand final, but Whyte's best is yet to come
text:
The 2026 NRL grand final was the kind of game they'll talk about for years to come.

As it goes further into history and the old stories come out at reunions and in front bars and on podcasts, they'll talk about Kalyn Ponga's try, Newcastle's heroic defence, Mark Nawaqanitawase's whole deal and the big finish.

They'll talk about James Tedesco winning the Clive Churchill Medal and maybe someone will remember his exact number of running metres — an obscene 388.

But what's certain is that at least one person will argue, passionately and adamantly, that Naufahu Whyte was the best player on the field.

Tedesco wins Churchill Medal After skippering the Sydney Roosters to their first men's premiership in seven years, James Tedesco claims the Clive Churchill Medal as the player of the match in the grand final.

There's no wrong answer between Tedesco and Whyte, who were the Roosters' best in the 19-18 victory.

Together, they combined for 55 runs and add Whyte's metres gained (187) to Tedesco's total and they carried the ball for more than half a kilometre.

Where Tedesco had 12 tackle busts, two forced dropouts and a try assist, Whyte forced several errors with his brutal defence, affirmed his status as one of the best forwards in the game and created the ruck speed that helped lead to Nawaqanitawase's crucial second-half try.

Winning the award as a middle isn't easy either, because even though you never win a comp without a few good ones, they always seem to miss out.

Sam Burgess was the last middle forward to win the Churchill medal when he led South Sydney from the front in 2014. Before then, you have to go back to Brent Kite in 2008 to find the last front-rower to do it.

For his part, the 24-year-old was happy to defer to his skipper.

Whyte and Tedesco were the premiers' two best players in the grand final win. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"He deserves it; he's been doing it all year," Whyte said.

"I have big love for my captain and what he's done for the game. I'll say he's the best fullback in the game ever. That's my brother."

While Tedesco took home the medal, Whyte's own trophy cabinet has become cluttered in a short space of time.

His premiership ring will vie with the Dally M Prop Of The Year award he won last week for pride of place, but if Whyte keeps up this form, there's sure to be more to come.

Especially if Whyte is telling the truth when he says there's still major improvement in him despite dominating on the game's biggest stage on Sunday night.

"I know this isn't my best. It's far from it. I'm still just at the start of my career. There's a lot of work to put in," Whyte said.

"In the grand final, I had to take it next level. It's not easy winning a grand final, and the Knights were always going to show up, so I had to push myself.

"Taking carry after carry, that's what I'll do for my brothers. It's paid off for me so far.

NRL grand final live A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final. Follow live.

"We came in confident we would get the job done, even down six, because that's the belief we have in each other, that's the belief we have in this team."

That belief proved crucial for the Tricolours as they claimed their first premiership since 2018-19, especially in coming back from 12-0 down with a Knights ambush eminently possible.

Whyte, who watches highlights of those games all the time, now has a version of it that he can not just replay but relive.

"Everything is going through my head and my heart now. I just want to embrace this moment and enjoy every part of it, because it's the best feeling ever," Whyte said.

"I screamed, had tears of joy; I was all over the place. All the hard work it took to get here — I'm speechless, brother, I really am."

title: Rising rates could 'bite' into Australian super, Bank of America warns
text:
What would it take to put the global economy into a tailspin?

The Bank of America, which is worth roughly $US275 billion ($395 billion), and dependent to a degree on functioning financial markets, is asking itself that question.

The answer lies in the cost of debt.

Low productivity, excess demand, the boom in artificial intelligence and the Iran war are all pushing up the cost of borrowing.

Despite this, interest rate increases have not yet done too much damage to share markets, property prices, or indeed many advanced economies.

But the Bank of America's head of interest rates strategy, Mark Cabana, has estimated the cost of borrowing, or level of interest rates, that would cause financial damage.

He says we're not far from that point.

Interest rates are still benign

The Federal Reserve is the US equivalent of Australia's Reserve Bank.

Bank of America's Mark Cabana says interest rates are "not restrictive" enough. (Supplied)

It recently raised America's benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to a range between 3.75 per cent and 4 per cent.

The trillion-dollar question many central banks are asking themselves is what interest rate level will work to lower overall demand in the economy?

And crucially, when does the cost of borrowing become financially dangerous?

Mr Cabana, who was previously an analyst at the New York Federal Reserve, said the recent US bond market sell-off had led to yields rising to multi-decade highs.

He also said the sell-off was not severe enough to cause steep falls in asset prices.

Bond yields rise when their prices fall.

Yields also rise ahead of increases to central bank interest rates.

"We expect that rates will continue to rise and that the curve will continue to flatten in the US, but also likely globally, simply because the level of interest rates today is not restrictive," Mr Cabana said.

Put simply, Mark Cabana does not believe US interest rates are currently high enough to significantly slow economic growth

"And what that means is that interest rates have not risen high enough to actually see any type of slowing in macroeconomic data.

"So it seems like the market is generally comfortable with the extent of the rate move thus far."

US interest rates heading higher

Goldman Sachs has pushed its forecast for the next US interest rate hike to December.

Bond market screaming economic trouble ahead Bond yields are the highest they've been in 20 years as inflation fears rip through global financial markets.

It did this after a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading last week cooled expectations the Federal Reserve would ‌hike rates again in October.

A December rate hike would push the fed funds target to 4 per cent to 4.25 per cent.

This interest rate level, Mark Cabana believes, is approaching the economic and financial danger zone, with greater concerns if expectations push into the high 4s and mid 5 per cents.

"That might be more consistent with some signs that we start to see a tightening of financial conditions and slowing in macroeconomic growth," he said.

Interest rate tipping point

Australia is already seeing a cooling of the housing market, and the share market is also well off its August highs.

Crackdown on super ads Unlicensed telemarketers who cold call and make unsolicited approaches to consumers to convince them to switch their super will be banned under long-awaited reforms.

The Australian government's 10-year bond yield — or the interest rate it needs to pay to borrow money for a decade — has risen to its highest level since 2011.

All working Australians would be mindful of this because it has direct implications for their superannuation balances.

Mr Cabana recently visited Sydney to, among other things, address the nation's superannuation heavyweights.

"I know that they are extremely focused on this question as well [of when interest rates will be restrictive to growth]," he told The Business.

Loading

Australian superannuation funds have tens of billions of dollars' worth of Australian workers' cash tied up on Wall Street, including the big tech companies.

" Our guidance to them would be that they should become much more concerned if you do see that macro data continues to be strong and that financial conditions are not showing signs of caring. "

Put simply, Cabana is saying that if the US economy continues to grow, and inflation pressures persist, US interest rates will need to push higher.

"That will mean that [US interest] rates may need to rise further and rates that have a 5 per cent or 5.5 per cent level."

Inflation worry is front and centre

Others see more leg room for asset prices to stretch out.

Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu believes the investment boom underway, particularly in relation to artificial intelligence (AI), will overwhelm any short-term financial market gyrations.

"Past rate hiking cycles have taught investors tough lessons, especially 2022, when the Fed lifted rates from near zero to above 4 per cent in nine months, and to above 5 per cent by mid-2023," she said.

"Equities fell because rising rates hit valuations before company profits could catch up."

Anna Wu says investors need to be "risk aware". (Supplied)

Ms Wu believes this time is different.

"We are in a slightly different regime now," she said.

"Bond markets expect inflation to stay around its five-year average.

"That means US yields are rising largely because investors expect stronger growth, not runaway prices."

Anna Wu draws the distinction between inflation worries and interest rates responding in a healthy way to the growing US economy.

"Investors should be risk aware," she said.

But as Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock put it last week, when asked if the RBA would need to push the economy into recession to achieve its inflation target, " I guess possibly."

She added that, "The scenario that I'm thinking of there is if inflation expectations get away from us.

"If that gets away, then that is a circumstance in which I think you might need to have quite a dramatic slowdown in the economy to — and that's our worry," Ms Bullock said.

It's clearly something Mr Cabana and the Bank of America are worried about too.

title: Yeo makes World Cup call, Walker earns Kangaroos spot
text:
Isaah Yeo will delay pectoral surgery to be captain for Australia's Rugby League World Cup campaign, after coach Kevin Walters unveiled a 23-man squad that includes Sydney Roosters halfback Sam Walker.

One of six debutants in the squad, Walker will be locked in a four-way battle with Cameron Munster, Tom Dearden and Mitchell Moses for a spot in the Kangaroos' halves.

Brisbane star Reece Walsh was also selected in Walters' squad and will compete with Clive Churchill medallist James Tedesco for the fullback role.

Roosters celebrate in Bondi Grand final hero Mark Nawaqanitawase lifts the Provan-Summons trophy to adoring fans as his coach describes the Roosters star as "extraordinary".

Latrell Mitchell has also returned to the Test team after battling injuries over recent seasons.

The losing grand finalists, Newcastle, are also represented in the squad, with Bradman Best one of the debutants.

"I'm really happy with the balance of the squad," Walters said.

"We have some real strike power and a significant amount of experience, along with size, power and speed.

"This will be a huge test. I have never before seen the amount of talent spread across the top nations. We are going to need to be at our best to take out the World Cup."

Kangaroos squad:

Bradman Best, Jack Bostock, Blake Brailey, Pat Carrigan, Lindsay Collins, Reuben Cotter, Tom Dearden, Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, David Fifita, Harry Grant, Keaon Koloamatangi, Liam Martin, Latrell Mitchell, Mitchell Moses, Cam Munster, Cam Murray, Jacob Preston, Kotoni Staggs, James Tedesco, Tom Trbojevic, Sam Walker, Reece Walsh, Isaah Yeo

AAP/ABC

title: Tom Cruise movie Digger bombs at box office, Verity takes top spot
text:
Movie star Tom Cruise has suffered one of the worst debuts of his career, with his new movie Digger flopping at the box office during its opening weekend.

Digger finished in fifth place at the North American box office with $US8 million ($11.5 million).

This was against a production budget of a reported $US125 million ($179.7 million) prior to marketing costs, which are believed to have been about $US100 million ($143.8 million).

Worldwide, the film pulled in $US20 million ($28.7 million), including $US12 million ($17.2 million) internationally.

Cruise is unrecognisable in the movie, which is a satire about a powerful oil tycoon whose reckless drilling triggers an environmental disaster.

It is directed by Academy Award-winning filmmaker Alejandro G Iñárritu and distributed by Warner Bros Pictures.

The abysmal opening comes just as Paramount Skydance is closing its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery after the US justice department greenlit the merger.

Sophie Wilde kept Tom Cruise's secret Less than a decade ago, Sophie Wilde was graduating from NIDA. Now she's rubbing shoulders with Tom Cruise in one of the most anticipated and divisive movies of the year.

Cruise has long been one of the most bankable stars in Hollywood and won an Honorary Oscar in 2025 for his extraordinary contributions to cinema.

He has spent most of the last decade as a top action hero starring in Mission: Impossible movies and Top Gun: Maverick.

The 64-year-old's last major box-office disappointment was 2017's The Mummy, which grossed $US409.2 million ($588.5 million) worldwide on a $US195 million ($280.4 million) budget.

Digger was both panned and lauded by critics, with some calling it a strained climate change farce.

To help sell the film, Cruise granted his first lengthy magazine interview in years.

Verity comes in at #1

Number one at the box office was Amazon MGM Studio's Verity, adapted from a Colleen Hoover novel.

Anne Hathaway plays Verity Crawford. Her husband Jeremy is played by Josh Hartnett. (Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios)

It is about a struggling author hired as a ghostwriter for a publishing sensation under eerie circumstances and stars Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett.

It is directed by Michael Showalter.

Verity treads on fertile ground From Misery to Yellowface, books and films about writers are favourites among the authors who pen them, but audiences love them too. Enter Verity.

It debuted with $US32.6 million ($46.8 million) in North America and was number one in Australia with $US3.1 million ($4.4 million), according to Box Office Mojo.

Final weekend box office figures are yet to be released, but below is what Rentrak has recorded so far in US and Canadian theatres.

1. Verity, $US32.6 million.

2. Resident Evil, $US12.5 million.



3. Heart of the Beast, $US11 million.



4. Primetime, $US8 million.



5. Digger, $US8 million.



6. Forgotten Island, $US7.2 million.



7. Avengers: Endgame: Encore, $US4.4 million.



8. Drishyam: The Conclusion, $US2.7 million.



9. Practical Magic 2, $US2.7 million.



10. Spider-Man: Brand New Day, $US2.5 million.

title: Property downturn worsens with less than 50pc of auctions leading to a sale
text:
Australia's auction clearance rate has slumped to a three-month low, while new data shows the number of unsold homes has surged by more than 20 per cent in the past year.

Less than half the auctions that occurred across the country last week resulted in a successful sale.

The preliminary clearance rate in the past week fell to 48.2 per cent, its lowest since late June (47.4 per cent) and the second-lowest preliminary reading for the year so far.

It has also been hovering at or below the 50 per cent mark for several months, coinciding with a steep decline in property prices and weak sentiment in the housing market.

In the past week, 1,223 auctions were held in the nation's capital cities.

So there were 12.8 per cent fewer auctions than the previous week. It was also a significant 47.5 per cent drop from a year ago, according to new data from property research firm Cotality.

Less than half the homes that hit the market and went to auction sold in the last week, Cotality data shows. (Supplied: Cotality)

Sharp fall in number of auctions held

Tim Lawless, Cotality's research director, said the weak result came off the back of long weekends in some states and the Reserve Bank's decision to lift interest rates for a fourth time this year.

It also comes after changes in this year's federal budget that sent shock waves through the property sector, including heavily restricted negative gearing, and in many cases higher capital gains tax for sellers.

Preliminary clearance rates across the major capitals last week compared with previous years. (Supplied: Cotality)

Sydney and Melbourne "have been a drag on the national result", Mr Lawless said.

In Sydney, 304 auctions were held in the past week, down 61 per cent to the week before. It was also a 38.5 per cent drop compared to a year ago.

There were 670 auctions held in Melbourne. That was a 136 per cent jump compared to the previous week when the city was having the AFL grand final long weekend.

But in the past 12 months, the number of auctions held in Melbourne has dropped 45.6 per cent, the largest decline of any capital city.

Tim Lawless says clearance rates have hit a three-month low. (ABC News: Jessica Ross)

Property taking up to six months to sell

Another real estate analysis firm, SQM Research, also released new data, showing some homes were sitting unsold on the market for as long as six months.

Homes that sat unsold for more than 180 days were clogging the market, with 10.5 per cent more older listings compared to a year ago.

Old housing stock is clogging the market. (Supplied: SQM Research)

Spring's traditional selling boom has ground to a halt so far this season, with the number of unsold homes across the country totalling 276,000 — a 21.6 per cent annual increase.

"The bulk of the increase is property that has been on the market for one to six months and hasn't sold," SQM research director Louis Christopher said.

"In Sydney, fewer vendors are listing than a year ago, yet total stock is up almost a fifth. That's a demand problem, not a supply surge."

The housing market is slumping and experts warn more falls are to come. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Forced sales on the rise

Brisbane and Adelaide have had the largest increase in the number of properties available for sale, up 43.5 and 39.5 per cent respectively, according to SQM's data.

Melbourne, meanwhile, had 30.3 per cent more homes up for sale than it did a year ago.

Perth's figure was up 21.3 per cent, while Canberra's was up 17.8 per cent.

SQM's figures also showed there were 4,872 distressed sales across Australia in September, which was a 29 per cent jump compared to the same period last year.

It follows the ABC reporting last week that Australian housing values had dropped for a sixth straight month, with many economists warning there will be further price falls ahead.

Mr Lawless said Australian households were "deeply pessimistic" about the cost of living crisis, interest recent hikes and the budget's changes to property taxes creating "less favourable conditions".

"Homes are taking longer to sell, auction clearance rates have held below average and advertised stock levels have risen across many markets," he said.

title: 'We'll be there': Fans rally behind Knights after grand final loss
text:
Newcastle Knights faithful say they remain proud of the team's efforts, despite a heartbreaking one-point loss to the Roosters in Sunday's NRL grand final.

Momentum had been building across Newcastle for the past week, with the city awash in red and blue as anticipation grew for the Knights' first grand final in 25 years.

Thousands of passionate fans gathered at the Knights' home ground last night to cheer on the side at a makeshift live site.

Meanwhile, bars, clubs and living rooms across the Hunter were packed with supporters decked out in red and blue.

The Knights started strong, scoring two tries in the first half to take a six-point lead into the break, but the Roosters took control in the second half, with a 69th-minute Daly Cherry-Evans field goal ultimately paving the way for the win.

Thousands of Knights fans watched the game from the team's home ground. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

Fighting back tears, Knights superfan Donna said it was a devastating loss, but the boys still did the town proud.

"[I'm] shattered but the team played so well, they really fought for it," she said.

"They really tried hard and we're really proud of the boys and everything they've achieved this year.

" We'll be there to cheer them back into home because they are everything to this town. "

Knights coach Justin Holbrook praised the side's "heart".

"If you can win anything on heart and effort, then we definitely won that because it was the hardest game of footy I've ever coached," he said.

"But again, you don't win off being proud, you win off being the better side, and we weren't the better side and we didn't win."

More patients discharged

The excitement building ahead of the grand final was shaken on Saturday when a car hit 10 fans lining the roadside in Newcastle to wave the Knights off to Sydney.

In the latest update, Hunter New England Health said six patients had been discharged from hospital.

One patient remains in a serious but stable condition and it is understood the other three are stable.

A five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man were both in critical condition on Saturday, but their conditions have improved overnight.

Hunter New England Health could not confirm which patient remained in the serious condition.

The 18-year-old alleged driver has been formally refused bail. (ABC News)

The alleged driver of the car, 18-year-old Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, is facing nine charges including three counts of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm.

He was formally refused bail on Sunday and is due to face court again later this month.

Knights faithful Kylie told the ABC the incident sent a shock wave through the community but ultimately brought it closer together.

"It just goes to show how close a community everyone is," she said.

" We all just support each other, that's just how Newcastle is. "

Ponga's try was a magnificent grand final moment. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Eyes to 2027

Newcastle captain Kalyn Ponga said he could not be prouder of his club's journey after finishing bottom of the ladder last year.

"Nothing this week was a burden on us," he said.

"Our community just rally around each other.

"Fortunately we get to experience what we experienced this week and that's definitely a feeling that I'll chase again."

Knights veteran and two-time premiership player Mark Hughes said the city would now turn its attention to next season.

"[I] can't wait to see the boys and give them a hug and say thank you for the hope and the joy they've given this community the last month," he said.

"Everyone around the stands are so proud of the boys' efforts.

" We're going to be back next year … the future looks so bright for the Knights. "

The Knights returned to Newcastle in the early hours of Sunday morning and were met with crowds of supporters and Newcastle chants reverberating through the streets.

Despite the loss, Knights fans will get the chance to celebrate the team's efforts with a fan day being held at Hunter Stadium later today.

title: Mary Fowler's Man City boost with big WSL win over Arsenal
text:
Manchester City may be a club in turmoil but Mary Fowler and her teammates have helped offer the beleaguered outfit a hint of a smile as England's women's champions continue their dominating start in the Women's Super League.

On Sunday (Monday AEST), Fowler came on as a second-half substitute and helped provide some spark as champions City went on to hammer one of their biggest rivals, Arsenal, 4-2 at home.

City stays perfect after five matches and still leads the WSL table by two points from Chelsea.

But it is proving a tough time for Arsenal and their three Australian European champion players from 2025 as the Gunners slipped 10 points off the pace in lowly 10th position.

Lauren Hemp scored twice for City as they twice came from behind to prevail, with the real spark coming when Fowler — making her 100th appearance for the club — was introduced just after the hour mark.

Fowler was joined on the park by Kerstin Casparij and Iman Beney with the home side trailing 2-1.

Within a minute, Casparij had equalised before Hemp put them in front for the first time nine minutes later and the league's top striker, Bunny Shaw, made it four with her fifth goal of the season.

Man City appeal guilty findings Manchester City denies the Premier League's finding that it used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs.

The dominance in the WSL has been a bright spot for City, which has filed an appeal against an independent commission ruling that found the club guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.

The EPL said last week that City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.71 billion) over nearly a decade.

For Arsenal, without a win since the opening day of the season, it was a second-straight defeat after losing 1-0 away to Chelsea last week.

It is a difficult time for the Aussie international trio at Arsenal, with Kyra Cooney-Cross just returning to the team on her soccer comeback, Steph Catley having been struggling with injury and Caitlin Foord yet to score this season while being played mainly as a substitute.

It was Foord's foraging in the box that forced the mistake which gifted Arsenal's second goal to Alessia Russo.

Yet the Gunners could have no complaints about slipping further adrift as, elsewhere, Chelsea, driven along by Ellie Carpenter in her more attacking vein this season, defeated West Ham 3-0.

Melvine Malard, Keira Walsh and Maika Hamano all scored for the Blues.

It came on a day when London City ‌Lionesses, without the injured Alanna Kennedy — who will miss the Matildas' upcoming internationals against Germany and Haiti — handed out a 6-1 thrashing to Tottenham Hotspur, including a double for Spanish great Alexia Putellas.

London is now third on 12 points, but Emily van Egmond could do nothing to help Charlton avoid a 5-1 hammering at Brighton as they sought in vain to earn their first point since promotion.

Plans to replace an older unit block with an $85 million luxury apartment complex on Oxford Street in Paddington have been approved by the Minns government despite concerns from hundreds of residents, the local MP and Woollahra Council that it would result in fewer relatively affordable homes. Citing the delivery of more than 40 well-located dwellings, the state government approved developer Toohey Miller’s proposal to bulldoze a three-storey block of 27 studio apartments and several townhouses for an eight-storey building of 44 units opposite the Victoria Barracks military base in Sydney’s east. The eight-storey block that Sydney developer Toohey Miller is proposing includes double-storey penthouses. Smart Design Studio Eleven of the new units will be affordable housing offered at below-market rent for 15 years, which triggered criticism the development would lead to an overall loss of moderately priced homes. Independent Woollahra councillor Harriet Price, who represents the Paddington ward, said tenants at the 50-year-old apartment block approved for demolition had last week “[woken] to the sound of a large truck delivering building materials and hoardings to the development site”.

Advertisement

Advertisement

The bulk of 377 public submissions the government received on the proposal were negative. Of the 332 objections, 80 per cent raised concerns the building would be at odds with Paddington’s character, while 69 per cent were worried about the loss of low-cost or affordable housing. Woollahra Council objected to the net loss of affordable dwellings and lack of smaller apartments; the height, bulk and scale of the “incompatible” building; traffic congestion and negative impacts on the Paddington heritage conservation area and Victoria Barracks. The existing apartment block on Oxford Street, opposite Victoria Barracks. Louise Kennerley In response to the feedback, the developer submitted revised plans which added four apartments, changed the dwelling mix to include one-bedroom units, and cut the building height by 1.2 metres. The Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure recommended the project for approval subject to conditions. Its assessment report said the block’s bulk and scale aligned with state planning controls for the site, would not have unreasonable privacy or overshadowing impacts, was compatible with the desired future character of the area, and would not adversely impact heritage.

“Low-income earners and vulnerable people are already getting evicted from their homes and neighbourhoods – just so that property investors and speculators can increase their profits.” Greenwich said the decision exposed “serious flaws” in the Labor state government’s planning policies and priorities. title: What are the Bombers still fighting for? It’s time to let Merrett go
text:
Advertisement

SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion What are the Bombers still fighting for? It’s time to let Merrett go Sam McClure Sports reporter October 5, 2026 — 3:36pm

October 5, 2026 — 3:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a point in any negotiation when resolve begins to look like stubbornness. When holding firm ceases to be a demonstration of strength and instead becomes an exercise in proving that strength exists. Essendon are approaching that point with Zach Merrett. Essendon president Andrew Welsh. Getty Images The former skipper wants to leave (again). Hawthorn want him (again). Essendon know it. Everyone in football knows it. So what, exactly, are the Bombers still fighting for?

Advertisement

President Andrew Welsh has again talked tough, warning Hawthorn not to “fumble” negotiations, not to get “too cute” and declaring that Essendon “won’t be crumbling”. He reminded Hawthorn that Merrett is Essendon’s best player. That he is contracted. That last year’s attempt to prise him out of Tullamarine failed. Zach Merrett wants to be traded to Hawthorn. Getty Images All true. But none of it changes the most important fact in this entire saga: Merrett wants out.

Advertisement

At some point the Bombers need to stop trying to win the negotiation and start trying to win again. There is a difference. The Bombers have spent too much of the past two decades fighting battles that ultimately haven’t taken them anywhere. They have changed coaches, chief executives, presidents, football bosses and strategies. They have defended their people, sacked their people, promised patience and demanded standards. Still, the drought goes on. But now they have a choice. They can spend another trade period arguing over precisely what a 31-year-old Merrett is worth, extracting every last drop from Hawthorn and telling the football world they will not be pushed around.

Advertisement

Or they can make the deal, take the picks and move forward. Hawthorn’s opening offer this year, of picks 15 and 25 and a future third-round selection, was rejected. Fine. It was an opening bid. Essendon are entitled to ask for more and Hawthorn should expect to pay a premium for a contracted champion. Merrett requested a move to the Hawks in 2025 but was unsuccessful. Getty Images But this cannot become another exercise in institutional pride. Merrett has given Essendon more than enough.

Advertisement

He has won seven Crichton medals. He has carried the club through some of the bleakest years in its history. He stayed when leaving would have been understandable. He performed while administrations changed around him and September success remained perpetually on the horizon. Now, at 31, he wants the opportunity to chase something Essendon have been unable to give him: a premiership. Holding him to his contract might be Essendon’s right. That doesn’t make it right for Essendon. And there is an irony here that should not be lost on anyone. More than two decades ago, Essendon and Hawthorn played the famous “Line in the Sand” game.

Advertisement

Perhaps it is time for the Bombers to draw another one. Not with Hawthorn – for themselves. Draw a line underneath the Merrett era. Draw a line underneath the idea that refusing to trade a player somehow proves you are a powerful football club. Draw a line underneath the obsession with winning the argument. Strong clubs don’t need to constantly tell everyone they’re strong. They make hard decisions and live with them.

Advertisement

Related Article Live

AFL 2026 AFL trade period day one: Saints put hefty price tag on ruckman; Pies secure Hogan and farewell Pendlebury Welsh says Hawthorn underestimated Essendon and “where we are going”. Good – then go there. If Essendon genuinely believe in their direction, the departure of one 31-year-old midfielder – even one as decorated and important as Merrett – cannot be allowed to derail it. Take the best deal available. Turn those selections into players who can be part of Essendon’s next serious premiership push. Give the next generation ownership of the football club, and let Merrett go.

Advertisement

That doesn’t mean giving Hawthorn whatever they want. It doesn’t mean rolling over. And it certainly doesn’t mean accepting an inadequate deal simply to make the problem disappear. Negotiate hard, but get a deal done. Because there is a difference between driving a hard bargain and holding a player hostage to make a point. Essendon need to decide what matters more: proving to Hawthorn that they cannot be bullied, or building the football club that Welsh insists is coming. title: ‘He’s outstanding’: Why George Gregan has been blown away by an 11-Test Wallabies halfback

He only made his Test debut a little over a year ago and has just 11 caps for the Wallabies, but halfback Ryan Lonergan has already impressed great Wallabies No.9 George Gregan so much he views him as one of Australia’s most valuable players, and even likened the Canberra star to iconic South African Fourie Du Preez. Praise for Lonergan also came from another World Cup winning star, with Dan Carter saying his maturity and leadership can help compensate for the Wallabies’ problems at five-eighth. After enduring a 93-game, nine-season wait for a Test debut, the 28-year-old finally got his shot off the bench at Eden Park last year. Lonergan will be back at the All Blacks’ fortress again this week, but this time he will be wearing the No.9. He grabbed the jumper in July following injuries to Jake Gordon and Tate McDermott and, based on subsequent form, Lonergan won’t be handing it back any time soon.

With a strong passing game, the Brumbies skipper has been instrumental in marshalling the Wallabies’ red zone attack. Lonergan’s kicking game has also been high quality, be it long, contestable or off the tee. The right-footer has kicked 30 of 33 goals since July. Ryan Lonergan takes on the Springboks in Perth. He has become a key player for the Wallabies in a short period of time. His only blemish was one of the four yellow cards. “He’s outstanding,” Gregan said. “He’s always had a really good skill set; he’s been a very good player for a number of years. He’s been knocking on the door. The door opened and he’s run through it.

“That performance [against the Springboks] was outstanding. I know Tate is there as well, and that competition’s good. They’re different, they provide different options. “The way Ryan controlled that game on the weekend, it really took a lot of pressure off the 10. Ryan Lonergan makes a break against Japan in Townsville. Getty Images “He really took a lot of responsibility. He can play both sides of the ruck, which I always love. It’s basic, it’s a fundamental. A good nine can scan and play both sides. “And his kicking game, short and long, it’s really balanced. He only missed a goal. It was an unbelievable performance.

“I was on a pod[cast], talking to [former Springbok captain] John Smit … and I said, ‘Mate, there was a glimpse of Fourie Du Preez there.’ It had that kind of look to it, and I don’t think I can give a bigger rap than that.” Du Preez, who starred in the Boks’ 2007 World Cup win, is rated by many Test players as one of the best No.9s of the modern era, along with Gregan. Eddie Jones said it was like having an extra coach on the field when Du Preez was playing. Fourie Du Preez scoring for the Springboks in 2015. Getty Images Despite his lack of experience at Test level, Carter said Lonergan could prove crucial to the Wallabies at the World Cup if they can’t find a consistent No.10. “You want some stability there, but if you’re not going to have an experienced 50 to 100-cap No.10, you’ve got to have a really stable No.9, and a solid midfield partner,” Carter said.

“And they [the Wallabies] have got the talent there. I’ve been really impressed with Ryan Lonergan, and just the way he leads out on the field. Gregan said the key for Lonergan was to carry through one of his strongest traits at the Brumbies to Test level: “It’s just about backing it up and being consistent, and he definitely has that.” Meanwhile, the Australian under-18 side has recorded a fourth straight victory over the New Zealand Schools team with a 40-33 win in Hamilton. title: With one last magic moment, DCE shows he’ll be a Hull of a big loss for the NRL
text:
Advertisement

SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion With one last magic moment, DCE shows he’ll be a Hull of a big loss for the NRL Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist October 5, 2026 — 3:30pm

October 5, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Daly Cherry-Evans kicked 28 field goals in 352 games for Manly, many of them match-winners. To see him do it in a grand final for the Roosters would have evoked mixed feelings for the Sea Eagles, but seriously? He gave so much to Manly, keeping them competitive year after year and week after week, often single-handedly (and double-footedly with those drop-kicks off his left or right), that it’s a bit amnesic to begrudge him the joy of going out a winner. Loading His recruitment, like Cooper Cronk’s in 2018, proved the difference for the Roosters in 2026. Fifteen years apart, Cherry-Evans owned two grand final nights. Hull have got a good one. Are all clubs created equal?

Advertisement

The Roosters will just have to live with the fact that most of the rugby league community don’t believe they, already premiership contenders, were able to recruit Cherry-Evans and Reece Robson and remain under the salary cap. I don’t think they’ll struggle with it. Another premiership trophy offers pretty warm comfort and a high hill to crow from. But in these polarising times, it’s difficult to imagine a grand final with two more divergent potential narratives. The Roosters’ NRL and NRLW teams celebrate their premierships together. Audrey Richardson Newcastle win, from last to first, and it gives every club heart. The Roosters win, and it suggests that the salary cap is not stopping wealthy clubs from hoarding talent. The Roosters’ counter-argument is that Naufahu Whyte, Rob Toia, Sam Walker and many more of its representative stars are one-club players; by which logic, Penrith wouldn’t have had to let go Stephen Crichton, Matt Burton, Jarome Luai, James Fisher-Harris and Viliame Kikau ... The margin might have only been one point in Sunday’s grand final, but the broader fan sentiment is very black and white. Not since David Gallop was chief executive has the NRL responded seriously to concerns about the failure of the cap to help equalise the talent pool.

Advertisement

It’s a bit tough to swallow any “fans first” rhetoric while some clubs remain, like George Orwell’s animals, more equal than others. Bring back the entertainment It’s a rule of every sporting event that there has to be a “random Souths guy”, and on Sunday night, that role fell to Jai Arrow. Retired South Sydney player Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles take part in a lap of honour. Getty Images In all the debate about how appropriate it was to have a sad and sombre moment as pre-grand final “entertainment”, and the inevitable last squeeze of shared sentiment to take it across the line into sentimentality, there wasn’t much about the Souths-ness of the situation.

Advertisement

A 100-game Rabbitoh was the centre of attention on the Roosters’ big night. In terms of tribalism, I’m not sure who was more put off: Souths, for having their man headline a Roosters game, or the Roosters, for having their grand final thunder stolen by someone from their enemy. Of course, Arrow’s diagnosis with motor neurone disease has transcended tribalism and brought rugby league together. But tribalism is more resilient and permanent than individuals, and the best that can be said about Arrow’s lap of honour, accompanied by Nathan Charles (a former rugby player with the same horrible disease), is that the league was making the best of a bad situation. With any luck, it will be a one-off, and the NRL will get its act together sooner about what it organises for its big night. Ali Brigginshaw was emotional after the Brisbane Broncos grand final defeat to the Roosters on Sunday. Getty Images Brigginshaw will always be game’s first champion Ali Brigginshaw, after nine seasons for the Broncos, four premierships, 13 Origins for

Queensland and 29 Tests for Australia, retired after the NRLW grand final with a legacy as the foundation stone of women’s rugby league in this country.

Advertisement

She is to the sport what Betty Wilson was to women’s cricket and Fanny Durack was to women’s swimming. As that first great champion, she can never be superseded. Brigginshaw’s final act as a player was to get whacked in the head as she completed a tough offload, still on the attack, looking for points even after Brisbane were well beaten. What a career. The game will always owe her. Great Dane was a Kiwi all along Having watched Dane Gagai torment NSW in 23 Origin matches for a decade, I’m sure I’m not the only one who thought he was a Queenslander. Critical Resources has engaged a firm of exploration specialists with extensive on-the-ground experience to kick off a hunt for the structural keys to its gold projects in Suriname, South America. The company recently secured exclusivity over the Gonini and Greenstars projects in September, which sit in the Guiana Shield - a vast, ancient geological region in northern South America, stretching across Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and parts of Venezuela and Brazil. Its old greenstone belts host major gold deposits and are geologically related to West Africa’s prolific Birimian gold belts, which were joined to the Guiana Shield before the Atlantic Ocean opened. Critical Resources’ Gonini and Greenstars gold projects sit in Suriname’s Guiana Shield, a region known for major gold deposits. Subject to the deals completing, the ASX-listed junior will hold a 90 per cent interest in 199 square kilometres of granted gold exploitation rights. Critical has now brought in experts GexplOre to run a major structural and geophysical interpretation across Gonini and Greenstars, in addition to more than 6000 square kilometres of the surrounding greenstone belt. The savvy move marks a significant step for Critical, which says it is the first ASX-listed company in decades to explore for gold in the country.

‘Engaging them now means we can build our structural picture and help us screen further opportunities across the belt.’ Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither GexplOre is no stranger to the Guiana Shield, having worked on about 20 gold projects across Suriname, Guyana and French Guiana. Notably, the firm has provided structural work for G Mining Ventures’ impressive Oko West project in Guyana and Founders Metals’ Antino project in Suriname, a project that has seen Canadian major Gold Fields tip in C$77 (A$77.7) million for a 19.9 per cent stake. Critical’s study will be a two-stage affair. The first stage involves a detailed, property-scale interpretation over two priority target areas at the 164-square-kilometre Gonini project. The second is a lower-resolution review of the wider greenstone belt, designed to screen for further opportunities. The work will process satellite elevation and spectral data, tapping into Gexplore’s existing database, to map host rocks, shear and fault corridors, and folding events that are known to control gold mineralisation in the region. In a deeply weathered and forest-covered terrain where rock outcrop is scarce, a satellite-based structural study is a logical and low-cost first filter to identify settings that might host gold before committing to more expensive on-ground work.

The wider Guiana Shield is considered hot property for gold exploration, with recent coverage highlighting it as significantly underexplored while attracting fresh capital. The region’s gold sector is already a major economic driver for Suriname, with the United States Geological Survey noting gold production delivered US$2 billion (A$2.9B) in export revenue in 2024 and accounted for 79 per cent of the country’s total exports. Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “The Gonini and Greenstars projects give ASX investors a rare opportunity for exposure to the Guiana Shield greenstone belt in Suriname, and give us the opportunity to continue to grow our footprint within Suriname and the greater Guiana Shield. Gexplore brings structural experience from some of the most significant discoveries in the Shield, including G Mining Ventures’ Oko West in Guyana and Founders Metals’ Antino in Suriname.” The company’s ground sits within the same Marowijne greenstone belt that hosts Newmont’s 5.1-million-ounce Merian mine, 66km away and Zijin Mining’s Rosebel mine, some 88km away. title: Inside the building of a Boeing 737 – from scratch
text:
Advertisement

BusinessCompaniesAviation Inside the building of a Boeing 737 – from scratch Chris Zappone October 5, 2026 — 3:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Few aircraft are more closely watched than the Boeing 737. Since first rolling off the assembly line in 1967, it has been in continuous production, and more than 12,000 airframes have been sold. In the process, it has created a legacy that has defined modern air travel, shaping how airports are built and the business models of airlines. There are 10 main stages to the production of a Boeing 737. Chris Zappone Boeing 737s are everywhere in global aviation – comprising whole fleets in some cases, and making up the backbones of others, such as those of Qantas and Virgin’s domestic operations. In recent years, however, the world’s most important commercial airliner has received attention for another, troubling, reason. The 737 has been tainted by design defects and quality control failures, most notably highlighted by the tragic crashes of two 737 MAX 8 jets in 2018 and 2019, which led to a worldwide grounding and direct US Federal Aviation Administration production oversight.

Advertisement

Loading The aviation icon now sits at the centre of a crisis of trust, but is, in a way, a symbol of American – and even Western – manufacturing. The symbolism is underpinned by commercial realities. The other pressing reason the 737 gets so much attention is that the world’s airlines remain hungry for new, more efficient 737 MAX airframes. The MAX uses 20 per cent less fuel than previous versions of the 737. Boeing says the MAX line offers airlines greater profit potential and it averages 7 per cent lower operating costs with up to 14 per cent lower maintenance costs than its competitor. This masthead recently secured access to a Boeing factory (after lengthy negotiations with the company) in Renton, Washington state. The facility has been the home of 737 production since 1970. Ten ‘flow days’

Advertisement

The 737 begins life as the fuselage, shipped in by train from Kansas, where it’s made, and enters the factory. Fuselages arrive by rail, in the distinct green colour of their protective primer. From there, each fuselage is rolled and lifted into position in an elevated part of the factory, where it is inspected. Insulation, electronic, hydraulic, and mechanical parts are then installed. Fuselages fresh in by train from Kansas at Boeing’s Renton, Washington state, factory. Chris Zappone At this point, the fuselages are lined up closely three abreast as they undergo their first three “flow days” – a term for the station of production. It takes 10 flow days, with each day representing a specific stop along the assembly line for the fuselage – to put a 737 together. The first three comprise wiring (about 70 kilometres’ worth), and putting in hydraulic tubing, flight control cables, the dorsal fin, and the controls within the flight deck. A protective cover for the radar at the tip of the plane’s nose is also installed in this phase.

Advertisement

In somewhat confusing nomenclature, the flow days are usually longer than 24 hours. The pacing of production is designed with enough of a gap to allow for minor delays or unexpected changes. On day four, the fuselages are moved down from the upper level of the factory onto the floor. To get them into lines, a crane mounted in the ceiling of the enormous facility moves them through a special gap in the wall into three parallel floor assembly lines. A busy but orderly floor at Boeing’s Renton factory. Chris Zappone Here the fuselages are spread out nose to tail. The three floor assembly lines are called the West Line, the Central Line and the East Line. This year Boeing opened a North Line for 737 production. Based in Everett, Washington, the North Line will expand Boeing’s capacity to build 737 MAX-family jets to meet market demand, including a current order backlog of 4300.

Advertisement

In the Renton factory, movement by crane happens at night, and it takes about an hour per fuselage. The factory runs 24 hours a day year-round except Christmas and the Thanksgiving holiday in late November. Boeing 737s have been made at the factory for decades. Chris Zappone Compared with Airbus factories, Boeing’s shop floor is more densely filled with equipment, and seems more like a factory. Staff call out to each other over the machine sounds of production. Workstations where specialised tasks and technical problem-solving take place are positioned along the floor. Between the buildings, staff move on shuttles, cars and scooters. The train line bringing the fuselages from Kansas comes right through the campus. Flow day four is always the big one for the 737. This is when it gets its wings, horizontal and vertical stabilisers, and landing gear. (The winglets, or tips of wings that flare up and down, are primarily made at Boeing’s Melbourne facility in Fishermans Bend.)

Advertisement

From there, the plane can rest on its own weight and is ready for the next step, in which the toilets, galleys and water and wastewater tanks are installed. The side walls, overhead bins and forward galleys are installed the day after. Carpeting and seats come on day eight. Boeing installs the seats using a machine similar to a hay baler, or an inclined conveyor belt that takes the seats up three at a time into the door, where technicians receive them and install them in the plane. Despite delays in cabin seat availability and FAA certification in wide-body planes, seats for the 737 have had less complexity, and hence, fewer hold-ups. On day nine, the engines are installed and connected to the electronic and hydraulic systems. The factory floor. Chris Zappone

Advertisement

All up, it takes 15 days from the fuselage coming into the factory to the plane being completed and made ready for inspection by the purchasing airline. After that, test flights are conducted over central Washington state. Factory employees lunch within view of the planes in progress, either eating at canteens or bringing their own food, and sitting at lunch tables on the balcony overlooking the main action. The vast building also houses offices, which gives it a hive-like feeling. One Boeing employee said working in the office in this building was more fun simply because he could look out and see the planes being put together at scale. Elsewhere, executives at Hyundai Motor and Ford Motor have also flagged that dealers are asking for more battery-powered inventory to sell as customers come back. title: TV’s most fascinating experiment ends with an emotional gut-punch
text:
Advertisement

★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview TV’s most fascinating experiment ends with an emotional gut-punch Paul Kalina Updated October 5, 2026 — 3:10pm ,first published October 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

70 Up ★★★★ 70 Up brings to a close one of the most fascinating – and arguably the longest-running – shows in the annals of TV history. It started in 1964 with a group of 14 children from a cross-section of English society in the documentary Seven Up! It was there we met Cockney lad Tony, who at age seven planned to be a jockey; headstrong Jackie, who said she would marry a boy with money; and Paul, who was raised in a boy’s home and in reply to a question about his future education replied, “What’s a university?” Every seven years since, director and behind-the-camera interviewer Michael Apted returned to see how these playful children became feisty teenagers, then parents and eventually grandparents; how marriages were made and unmade; how hopes soared and were sometimes extinguished. John, Bruce, Symon, Andrew, Suzy, Jackie, Tony, Sue, Peter, Paul and Neil all return for 70 Up, reportedly the final instalment of this famous documentary series. ITV The original concept was to test the Jesuit adage, “Give me a child until he is seven and I will give you the man” – a window into how class and socioeconomic circumstances determine the chances and opportunities that shape their (and our own) lives. But what it’s mostly remembered for today is the front-row seat it offered to the daily dramas of life and how each of the participants was forged into the person that they became.

Advertisement

Now, here they are as 70-year-olds looking back, but also forwards, in what is touted to be the last instalment of the show. Related Article Review 63 Up's Aussie battler Paul Kligerman on the call he dreads every seven years In the two-part 70 Up, we see where the 13 surviving people have ended up (Lynn, the librarian, died in 2013). For the most part, they’re fulfilled, contented and self-aware – which may be surprising given the challenges some have faced. They are also deeply contemplative and ruminative, not only about how their lives have unfolded but how they’ve been depicted in the films. Directed by Asif Kapadia (Amy, Senna, Diego Maradona), 70 Up is very much about legacy (Apted died in 2021). At stake is not only the personal legacies of the participants, but the legacy of the series itself. Several talk about how the show has turned them into celebrities, and we are poignantly reminded that as seven-year-olds they never really consented to be part of a program that has come to define them. They all return, however, for this last hurrah – even some who opted not to participate in earlier instalments. Their humility and, ultimately, gratitude are truly heartrending.

Advertisement

Sue and Claire reflect on their past selves. SBS/ITV Indeed, 70 Up raises many valid questions about Apted’s agendas and preconceived ideas, such as the sexist questions he put to the female participants, as well as setting up the posh schoolboys to look like undeserving twits. “Sneering and supercilious” is how one of the participants remembers him. Hearing some of Apted’s loaded and insulting questions from earlier chapters is cringe-making. Editor's pick Australian TV ‘That’s got to count for something’: Julia Morris and Julia Zemiro on four decades in the spotlight That’s one part of the legacy that 70 Up wants to correct. The other is that the series’ focus on outdated notions of class and society meant it wasn’t always asking the right questions. It’s here that 70 Up, its second episode in particular, delivers an emotional punch to the gut. There’s Neil, the sunny daydreamer in Seven Up! who now talks with admirable candour about his lifelong mental health battles. And Symon, who still rues having never met his father, and has gone on to foster more than 100 children. What we take away isn’t the fairness of the cards they were dealt but how they faced the unpredictable twists and turns that life put in their paths. It’s impossible not to be moved by this remarkable endeavour.

For Pauline Moore, Melbourne’s tram network connected her to the world. From her home in Hawthorn, the 78-year-old could visit her grandson and buy her own groceries. She could travel to the local library, and make her own way to her regular dialysis appointments at the hospital. Pauline Moore passed away two months after she had a serious fall on a Melbourne tram. But in September 2022, Pauline broke her pelvis during a fall on the tram. Protocol required the immediate evacuation of the tram, and she was forced to call her own ambulance from the footpath, so the tram could be returned to the depot. It left the 78-year-old scared to ride public transport.

Advertisement

Then two months later, Pauline passed away from complications sustained in hospital after the fall. In the four years since her mother’s death, Cath Moore has been asking for greater transparency and accountability from Yarra Trams regarding its safety and first aid policies. Cath Moore’s mother fell on a tram and broke her pelvis. She died two months later following complications in hospital. Chris Hopkins “It’s not good enough … people fall through the cracks, and it’s the most vulnerable members of society who are the ones that should have the most protections afforded them,” Cath said. Between 2016 and 2025, 812 people were injured due to an incident on a Victorian tram, according to statistics from the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator. A further eight passengers died.

Advertisement

Pauline Moore passed away in November 2022, from complications sustained in hospital from a fall on a tram. But deaths like Pauline’s – which happened in the weeks following a fall and included other factors – aren’t necessarily reflected in these statistics. When the 78-year-old boarded a route 48 tram in Richmond, she didn’t have a chance to sit down or hold on before the tram started to move – then brake – and she fell over. The driver carried out a welfare check. Pauline indicated she’d hurt her back, but declined an ambulance at first, partly because she was in shock and disoriented from the fall. As it was a serious incident, Yarra Trams protocol meant that all passengers were unloaded from the tram so it could be sent back to the depot, where it could be inspected for defects and the driver would receive a welfare check.

Advertisement

That left Pauline to call her own ambulance soon after from the footpath. On arrival at the hospital, doctors found she had broken her pelvis. The grandmother was discharged, before later returning to hospital due to a previously undetected second break. During one of these stays, she contracted a bacterial infection – clostridioides difficile – which ultimately led to her death. “She kept saying to me in hospital: ‘If only [the driver] waited another few seconds’ … it haunts me to this day,” Cath said. Cath Moore wants Yarra Trams’ policies to be more accessible and transparent. Chris Hopkins Tram drivers do not need to undertake any first aid training or have medical supplies on board, according to a report by the Public Transport Ombudsman provided to Cath and seen by The Age. Drivers are required to check whether passengers need medical assistance, but aren’t required to call an ambulance if the passenger declines help.

While the ombudsman report indicated that changes had been made to the operator’s First Aid policies following Pauline’s death, the Yarra Trams spokesperson didn’t say what these changes entailed. The spokesperson said that the safety practices across the network are regularly reassessed. COTA Victoria supports mechanisms like pre-boarding ticket validation, increased on-board announcements and appropriate pauses when a passenger with accessibility needs is boarding or exiting. title: Medicinal cannabis company scrubs false claims after questions
text:
in brief MOCA admits its products were wrongly described as TGA-approved.

More than 99 per cent of medicinal cannabis products are not TGA-approved.

An online medicinal cannabis prescriber has admitted it wrongly described its products as approved by Australia's medicines regulator.

But it says it will only "consider" notifying clients about the change.

Medicinal Organic Cannabis Australia (MOCA) had claimed its entire product range was approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), whereas in fact the products it sells, while legal, are unapproved therapeutic goods and have not been assessed by TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.

Experts have told SBS News the claim is one example of concerns about how medicinal cannabis products are described and marketed to patients.

Earlier this year, the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) wrote to the TGA calling for reforms to the way medicinal cannabis is prescribed and regulated.
