Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

SBS investigation uncovers misleading claims

As part of its research into the online medicinal cannabis industry, SBS News found examples of clinics and online retailers using language that could give prospective patients the impression their cannabis products had been "approved" by the TGA.

One example was MOCA, which lists a Sydney address on its website.

Managing director Alessandro Sorbello stated on the website that the company's "complete product range is approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and is ready for practitioners to prescribe to patients in Australia".

The website also said its "approved medical cannabis product range includes capsules, sublingual oils, isolates, vape pens and whole cannabis flowers".

Source: SBS News

However, the TGA's Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) lists only two cannabis medicines as approved products: Epidyolex, an oral solution used for specific forms of epilepsy and Sativex, a mouth spray used for multiple sclerosis-related spasticity. Combined, these two products make up less than 1 per cent of medicinal products available in Australia.

In a statement to SBS News, MOCA acknowledged that the wording "did not accurately reflect the regulatory status" of its products and said it had removed it.

The company said it was also reviewing its broader website to ensure information about its products and their regulatory status was "accurate and consistent with current requirements".

Asked whether it would communicate the changes to patients, MOCA said it "will consider whether any further communication is appropriate as part of that process".

READ MORE Medicinal cannabis patients given green light to drive in NSW

In a statement to SBS News, a spokesperson for the TGA said it was unable to say whether the information identified by the investigation constituted unlawful advertising, saying advertising of therapeutic goods "must undergo robust assessment on a case-by-case basis and in the context in which it is viewed".

However, the regulator said the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 prohibits advertisements that imply a therapeutic good has been approved or recommended by the government or a government authority.

"Businesses are responsible for understanding and complying with their regulatory obligations when advertising and supplying therapeutic goods, including advertising through online platforms," the spokesperson said.

Calls to better regulate prescribing

More than 99 per cent of medicinal cannabis products in Australia are not included in the ARTG and have not been assessed by the TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.

However, this does not mean they can't be prescribed. Doctors can lawfully prescribe some of these unapproved but legal products through regulatory pathways, including the Special Access Scheme (SAS) and Authorised Prescriber Scheme (APS), subject to relevant requirements. The SAS allows doctors to access unapproved products on a case-by-case basis, while the APS doesn't require individual approvals.

Medicinal cannabis contains the same primary compounds found in cannabis more broadly, including THC, the main psychoactive compound and CBD, which does not produce the same intoxicating effects. Their strength, cannabinoid content and composition can vary between products.

The regulatory framework has also attracted scrutiny from the RACGP, which raised concerns about the prescribing of unapproved medicinal cannabis products in a submission to a TGA consultation.

The college said the system isn't working as it should and has called for changes.

"It is the view of the RACGP that the absence of ARTG processes leave Australians vulnerable to unsafe products and devices," the submission states.

Clarification: The headline of this story previously read: Medicinal cannabis prescriber scrubs false claims but won't notify customers. It has been updated to correct the description of the company and better reflect its position on notifying customers.

title: What Australia's medicinal cannabis boom isn't telling patients
text:
For Alex, getting a prescription for medicinal cannabis was remarkably simple.

The Sydney-based part-time worker had used cannabis recreationally for years, taking it to switch off and wind down after a hard day's work. She struggles with sleep, anxiety and depression, and says cannabis has significantly improved her quality of life.

"I'm aware it doesn't work for everybody ... but it's an amazing substance for me," she tells SBS News.

Friends who used medicinal cannabis later recommended the prescription route, and after researching providers online, she found a clinic offering what she describes as a "cheap, quick and easy" service.

But the evidence for using medicinal cannabis for conditions such as anxiety, insomnia and depression remains limited, with the Australian Medical Association saying there is little or no evidence base for some of these uses.

A decade after medicinal cannabis was legalised, prescribing has surged and a large commercial market has emerged in Australia. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

Alex's experience is increasingly part of the way Australians access cannabis. SBS News has withheld her surname for privacy reasons.

Ten years after medicinal cannabis was legalised, prescribing has expanded and a large commercial market has emerged around it. Australians aged 18 and over can access medicinal cannabis through online prescribing services, which patients can then take to a pharmacy.

But as access has grown, so too have concerns about how medicinal cannabis is prescribed and marketed, the evidence behind some of its uses and whether patients fully understand the products they are being prescribed.

What 'medicinal cannabis' really means

For patients, getting a prescription can make a cannabis product feel much like any other medicine. But the word "medicinal" does not necessarily mean a product has been assessed and registered by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA).

Most medicinal cannabis products in Australia are not included in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) and have not been assessed by the TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness.

However, doctors can lawfully prescribe some of these unapproved products through regulatory pathways, including the Special Access Scheme and Authorised Prescriber Scheme. Sponsors are also legally responsible for ensuring these products comply with applicable Australian standards, including requirements relating to quality and labelling.

Medicinal cannabis contains the same primary compounds found in cannabis more broadly, including THC, the main psychoactive compound and CBD, which does not produce the same intoxicating effects. Their strength, cannabinoid content and composition can vary between products.

READ MORE Medicinal cannabis patients given green light to drive in NSW

That regulatory distinction is central to the debate over medicinal cannabis, with some doctors and researchers questioning whether the language around the treatment can sometimes give greater weight to its medical benefits than the evidence supports.

Matthew Large, a conjoint professor from the School of Psychiatry at the University of New South Wales, says the term "medicinal cannabis" can overstate its benefits and downplay its risks.

[I believe] the medicalisation of cannabis is the biggest public health bungle in Australia's history.

"As a medicine, cannabis has not come with the appropriate health warnings. And because it's become a medicine, it's become more and more difficult to talk with patients about its harms around addiction and psychosis," he tells SBS News.

As part of its research, SBS News found examples of clinics and online retailers using language that could give prospective patients the impression their cannabis products had been "approved" by the TGA.

One example was online prescriber Medicinal Organic Cannabis Australia (MOCA), which lists a Sydney address on its website.

Managing director Alessandro Sorbello stated on the website that the company's "complete product range is approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and is ready for practitioners to prescribe to patients in Australia".

The website also said its "approved medical cannabis product range includes capsules, sublingual oils, isolates, vape pens and whole cannabis flowers".

In a statement to SBS News, MOCA acknowledged the wording "did not accurately reflect the regulatory status" of its products and said it had been removed.

The company said it was also reviewing its broader website to ensure information about its products and their regulatory status was "accurate and consistent with current requirements".

Asked whether it would communicate the changes to patients, MOCA said it "will consider whether any further communication is appropriate as part of that process".

The most common way medicinal cannabis was prescribed so far in 2026 was in herb or dried form. Source: Getty / NurPhoto

In response to questions from SBS News about the MOCA material identified by the investigation, a TGA spokesperson said the regulator was unable to say whether it constituted unlawful advertising.

The spokesperson said advertising of therapeutic goods "must undergo robust assessment on a case-by-case basis and in the context in which it is viewed".

However, the regulator said the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 prohibits advertisements that imply a therapeutic good has been approved or recommended by the government or a government authority.

Businesses are responsible for understanding and complying with their regulatory obligations when advertising and supplying therapeutic goods, including advertising through online platforms.

The ARTG lists only two cannabis medicines as registered products, including Epidyolex, an oral solution used for specific forms of epilepsy, and Sativex, a mouth spray used for multiple sclerosis-related spasticity.

Combined, these two products make up less than 1 per cent of medicinal products available in Australia. Other medicinal cannabis products are not listed on the ARTG.

A spokesperson for the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) told SBS News it has concerns "some registered health practitioners are prioritising profits over patient safety".

"Ahpra has put the medicinal cannabis industry on notice about its expectations and will continue to use data, including from other regulators, to identify and investigate practitioners who are not prescribing safely," they said in a statement.

Ahpra confirmed regulatory action had been taken against 80 practitioners since 2019 in relation to the prescribing or dispensing of medicinal cannabis.

Large says since the COVID-19 pandemic there has been an "explosion" in cannabis prescribing, particularly for anxiety and depression.

He argues that cannabis can make people feel calmer in the short term without necessarily treating the underlying condition.

His concern is particularly focused on products containing high levels of THC — the psychoactive component of cannabis.

He says THC's effects can be delayed, creating a gap between taking the drug and experiencing its negative effects.

This is a slow-moving problem with a delay between ingestion and toxicity.

Large points to research examining cannabis use and psychosis, saying the findings are concerning, and says the risk of psychosis may increase with greater cannabis exposure and potency.

Research has found an association between frequent use of high-potency cannabis and psychosis, although this does not establish that prescribed medicinal cannabis causes psychosis.

He also warns of the potential for dependence.

"I think it's quite possible that we are going to have a much greater proportion of our population addicted to yet another compound."

He stresses that not all medicinal cannabis products carry the same risks.

Low-THC products and topically applied products such as ointments are likely to be much less toxic, he says.

Concerns over prescribing

Melbourne-based Vicki Kotsirilos was among the first Australian GPs authorised to prescribe medicinal cannabis.

She initially obtained approval to treat patients suffering from chronic, severe cancer pain and neuropathic pain.

But a decade on, she is concerned about how easily some patients can obtain cannabis.

Prescribing medicinal cannabis should always be a last-resort treatment, after other non-cannabis options have been explored.

"We now have clinics and telehealth companies that solely prescribe cannabis to patients. That shows a lack of ethical guidance and professionalism," she tells SBS News.

Source: SBS News

Kotsirilos says the greatest concern is not necessarily CBD-dominant products, but products containing high levels of THC.

Australian medicinal cannabis products are grouped into five categories according to their cannabinoid content. Categories 1 and 2 are CBD-dominant; category 3 is balanced; and categories 4 and 5 are generally THC-dominant.

Kotsirilos says doctors need to be particularly cautious when prescribing high-THC products to people with conditions such as anxiety.

"THC can aggravate anxiety, can cause illusions and psychosis, and aggravate mental health conditions," she says.

She also warns that high doses can cause sedation and drowsiness and can lead to cannabis use disorder.

Kotsirilos says doctors should first consider behavioural and non-drug treatments, particularly when patients present with anxiety or sleep problems.

"For anxiety, it's really important to first deal with the patient's stresses in their lives, look at their behaviour, exercise, talk to them about sleep and how to correct sleep," she says.

Source: SBS News

If medicinal cannabis is ultimately prescribed, she advocates starting with lower doses and gradually increasing them where appropriate, while favouring CBD-dominant products over high-THC products.

The potency problem

Large says the potency of cannabis available today is substantially higher than that of cannabis that was commonly available decades ago.

"In the 1970s, illegal cannabis typically had THC concentrations of approximately 2 to 5 per cent at the very most," he says.

"It's possible now to ring up a doctor with a relatively minor complaint and get sent, within 24 hours, multiple scripts, some of which contain 35 per cent THC."

The availability of high-THC products is one reason he believes the risks of cannabis need to be communicated more clearly to patients.

There are so many misconceptions about the toxicity of cannabis.

That makes the language clinics use particularly important.

For patients, the word "medicinal" can suggest that a product has been rigorously tested, is proven to work and is safer than recreational cannabis.

But those assumptions do not necessarily follow from the fact that a product has been prescribed.

The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners has called for changes to the regulatory framework, including greater safeguards around prescribing, and has expressed concerns about how some products are accessed through telehealth services.

The appeal of access

For patients like Alex, however, the distinction between the benefits and risks can feel less complicated.

She says medicinal cannabis has helped with her health concerns, and that the cost of accessing it fits within her budget.

She had a free video call with a nurse, followed by a consultation with a doctor and subsequent appointments every few weeks or months.

Each doctor's appointment was substantially less than she would have paid at her private GP, which she says made the service attractive to her.

The accessibility did not mean the cannabis itself was necessarily cheaper.

Alex says the cost of the products themselves was comparable to cannabis she had previously bought illegally.

She was prescribed flower containing 25 per cent THC, as well as gummies and CBD oil.

Alex says her doctor was prepared to prescribe a higher-THC product because of her experience using cannabis recreationally.

She says she has not experienced the paranoia, dizziness or discomfort that can accompany cannabis use.

For Alex, the ease of accessing medicinal cannabis was part of its appeal. But experts say the question is whether patients are getting enough information to understand the potential benefits and risks.

title: Roosters defeat the Knights in a thrilling finish to claim 16th NRL premiership
text:
IN BRIEF The NRL grand final preshow featured a tribute to retired Rabbitoh Jai Arrow.

The Knights went up 12-0 early but the Roosters stormed back to win the grand final.

The Sydney Roosters are back on top of the NRL, coming from behind to claim their first premiership in seven years with a 19-18 defeat of Newcastle.

After trailing 12-0 just before halftime at Stadium Australia on Sunday night, the Roosters dominated the second half before holding on late for their 16th title.

The result ended a fairytale run for the Knights, who had ridden a wave of emotion after going from wooden spooners last year to enter the finals in seventh spot.

Rugby-bound winger Mark Nawaqanitawase scored a double, getting the Roosters on the board before halftime and backing it up with another with 20 to play.

Front-rowers Spencer Leniu and Naufahu Whyte were both great up front, while Daly Cherry-Evans slotted a field goal to make it 19-12 with 10 minutes to play.

It marked the 32nd and final one-pointer of Cherry-Evans' career, and proved the difference when Greg Marzhew crossed with three minutes to play.

The drop goal also ensured Cherry-Evans would finish his NRL career as the game's oldest premiership winner in 104 years.

Kalyn Ponga was the Knights' best, while Newcastle spent much of the game resiliently defending their own line before the pressure eventually told.

"The journey is all about the ups and downs and it's so amazing to finish here," Cherry-Evans said.

"I didn't want to sound arrogant or overly confident, but I had so much belief in this club, the players, the coach.

"This is what it's all about. And we did it. And I'm so, so proud to be here, and I just can't wait to go see my family."

The Roosters have been one of the NRL's heavyweights for 14 seasons under Trent Robinson, to the point where seven years without a title felt like an eternity.

Roosters claim double premiership with NRLW grand final win

The Roosters also won the NRLW grand final earlier on Sunday, beating the Broncos 30-6 at Sydney Olympic Park.

The Roosters, led by captain Isabelle Kelly, secured a strong lead against the Queenslanders, heading into the second half 26-0.

A testament to their discipline, the Sydneysiders were relentless in their defence against the Broncos.

Brydie Parker delivered a stellar performance, scoring a hat-trick with only 12 minutes left in the game.

Roosters prop, Millie Elliott, will retire with a premiership win after the Roosters defeated the Broncos at the 2026 NRLW grand final in Sydney. Source: Getty / Cameron Spencer

Roosters Corban Baxter and Millie Elliot are retiring from the league, leaving with a premiership under their belts after losing to the Broncos in 2025.

Broncos halfback scored a try in the final six minutes, with an assist by captain Tamika Upton.

It's the Barada woman and fullback's first season as captain, taking the reins from NRLW great Ali Brigginshaw, who led the team for eight years and is retiring at the end of the season.

In a post-match speech, Upton congratulated the Roosters on their win and expressed her condolences to the victims of the car crash in Newcastle on Saturday.

Roosters halfback Tarryn Aiken was named the Karyn Murphy medalist.

title: Why some Australians are turning to strangers for a taste of home
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

There's something about food that makes us feel cared for and at home.

For Michelle Raguz, the biggest compliment she can receive is being told her food tastes just like baka's (Croatian for grandmother).

"That was my aim, to get that nostalgia back," the mother-of-three tells SBS News.

Raguz, who lives in Austral in Sydney's south-west, is one of a growing number of people running small businesses from their home kitchens, often supplying niche cultural foods to families who may not have the time or skills to devote to make them, but still crave the taste of home.

While Croatian-style biscuits are available to buy in certain shops, the 41-year-old says "anything that comes out of a machine is not going to taste the way a homemade biscuit does".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

During her busiest periods ahead of Easter and Christmas, Raguz easily makes 1,000 biscuits for sale through her Instagram account.

Michelle Raguz sells freshly made biscuits and cakes on her Instagram account. Source: Supplied / @thewogbox

The NSW Food Authority tells SBS News that "anecdotal feedback from local councils indicates home-based food businesses have grown in number", although it does not specifically collect data on these businesses.

Driven by a mix of nostalgia, convenience and a desire for supportive communities, these micro businesses have also become a way for people to stay connected to their culture, share food traditions and recreate a sense of home.

Not everyone can bake mum's biscuits

Among the Balkan community in Australia, including those of Macedonian and Serbian heritage, it's traditional to enjoy treats like madarice (a chocolate layer cake) and oblatne (wafers) with coffee at social gatherings.

But Raguz says many older members of the Croatian community can no longer make the traditional biscuits and cakes she sells.

"Even my mother-in-law, she's got arthritis in her hands [so] they can't stand there and bake anymore," she says.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, she was spurred to start her business by a desire to help her community, which didn't have the option of having traditional foods delivered.

[During lockdowns] if you wanted to reach out to somebody, the only option people had were … donuts or flowers.

This was not appealing to Croatians, Raguz says, who love having small portions of a variety of homemade cakes and biscuits.

"We're biscuity people. You have a slice of this, or a piece of that."

Raguz spent nearly a year perfecting her almond moons to taste just like the ones her aunt made. Source: Supplied

About 90 per cent of her customers are of Balkan heritage, but she also has other customers who have found her sweet treats after friends or neighbours shared her biscuits with them, for example.

"I actually get a lot of Asians — once they try it, they love it."

Michelle Raguz (centre) says she loves cooking for her family and enjoys keeping Croatian food traditions alive. Source: Supplied

Raguz says she loves recreating the warm memories she had growing up and is lucky to have inherited a love of cooking from her mum.

"All of our friends still talk about my mother's hospitality," she says, adding that she always wanted to carry that on with her own children.

I don't want the way we grew up to be lost.

'Cooked by people that care'

Home cooking can create a sense of care that sets it apart from restaurant meals, says Carol Perdigao, a former chef who moved to Melbourne from Brazil six years ago.

She regularly orders food such as feijão tropeiro (bean stew) and empadão de palmito (palm heart pie) from a home cook via WhatsApp.

"It's something I miss from home," she says of the dishes, which she adds can be difficult to find in Brazilian restaurants in Australia that often focus on meat.

She says that when she began ordering the food she was mainly motivated by the desire to support the Brazilian community in Australia but says it is also "one of the best foods flavour-wise because it's cooked by people that care".

"A lot of people work in hospitality because they end up there and it's a very busy-paced life," Perdigao notes of restaurant cuisine.

"[You don't] necessarily get that sort of care with the food."

The meals have also helped Carol to continue the Brazilian tradition of having a large warm meal for lunch.

"It's an important part of the day for me," she says. "It's a habit that I really wasn't able to get rid of."

I basically don’t feel satisfied if I don’t eat a home-cooked lunch.

Cultural sociologist Sian Supski, a research fellow at Monash University, says food can be used to make people feel at home. She says women migrating to Australia in the 1950s used it as a way to become part of the Australian suburbs.

"They would give food to their neighbours and then their neighbours would ask for the recipes," she says.

Migrants must also find local substitutes for some ingredients and Supski says this creates a lot of "cultural traffic" between the place they now live and where they came from.

"So I think that food helps the placemaking [that helps people feel connected to spaces]."

'I feel like people appreciate me'

Sarah (not her real name) says the thing she values the most about selling her homemade dumplings is that it gives her a chance to meet her neighbours, and a topic to talk about.

"My job [in Australia is] pretty boring and not so many people talk [with me]," she tells SBS News.

"[But] I love chatting."

Sarah sees her dumpling business as just a hobby, which is why she doesn’t want her name to be published. She sells one or two bags of dumplings in Sydney each week, mostly through posts on a local community Facebook page.

"Back in China you have a good income; here you [are] basically nothing," she says.

Doing this just give me confidence. I feel like people appreciate me. I feel good for myself.

Sarah's jiaozi (northern Chinese-style dumplings) are a blend of how her grandma cooks and the preferences of her non-Chinese husband and two children.

The pork and prawn filling is minced by hand chopping, just like Sarah's grandma's, but she wraps them using store-bought dumpling pastry, which is thinner than handmade dough, and steams them rather than boiling them.

This also suits Sarah's customers as the majority of them are not Asian. Regular buyers include a woman who orders dumplings every Valentine's Day, and a man who buys them monthly to serve to his mates during a regular catch-up.

Sarah's jiaozi has helped her to get to know her neighbours. Source: Supplied

Once her children finish their education, Sarah says she may start a small dumpling bar because she loves having a drink and chatting with friends while eating dumplings.

"You know Chinese, we love sharing food," Sarah says.

"The way we show love [to] neighbours or that, we just keep feeding them. That's the Chinese."

Mother-of-three Asma Khalaf would also like to build up her business selling Middle Eastern treats in Sydney.

Khalaf arrived in Australia from Gaza two years ago and the 39-year-old says she wanted to find a way to talk about her background.

How can I show other people, who [are] in different culture, about my culture?

"Then I start thinking about food, because food is the main language to talk about your country."

A former teacher, Khalaf says she used to enjoy making pastries in her spare time before the war.

She's now selling these using Palestinian recipes inspired by her mother through an Instagram account. Eid is the busiest time for her and last year she made 13kg of fragrant treats like maamoul (date cookies), kaak (ring-shaped pastry) and baklava (layered filo pastry dessert).

Asma Khalaf sells Middle Eastern pastries such as maamoul and kaak on her Instagram page. Source: Supplied / @yafasweet__

While most of her goods are sold to those of Middle Eastern background, about 30 per cent are bought by people from other cultures.

Demand can be quite unpredictable but Khalaf hopes to eventually open her own shop, to help support her family in Australia and Gaza.

Supski says food can hold an important role for migrants from countries that have experienced societal upheaval and seen their cultural and literary heritage destroyed.

"They have lost their loved ones, or their connection because records have been lost, as well as people.

"The re-creation of food and the feeding of community is this very direct connection straight back to family or to the place that people grew up."

Concerns over food safety and commercialisation

But the Food Safety Information Council has warned Australians not to buy or sell food through social media sites that is prepared in unregulated home kitchens.

Chief executive officer Lydia Buchtmann says food prepared in a home kitchen or backyard barbecue is unlikely to meet the food safety regulations that apply to businesses selling food.

A NSW Food Authority spokesperson tells SBS News home-based food businesses must meet the same requirements as all food businesses in NSW.

"Home-based businesses must notify the appropriate authority, their local council or the NSW Food Authority, with their business details so their food safety compliance requirements can be assessed," the spokesperson says.

READ MORE The costly contradiction hiding in Australian kitchens

Sukhmani Khorana of the University of NSW, whose research looks at how migrants use food cultures to foster belonging, says food safety verification is important, although she questions whether it's always accessible to the people starting these businesses.

"Sometimes it also doesn't matter a great deal to customers from the same community if they know the family," she tells SBS News.

She says she's also noticed an increase in supper clubs, where people host guests in their homes, which can allow for specific foods from certain regions to be experienced in place of cuisines often served in restaurants catering to broader tastes.

But Khorana notes there is always a potential downside to commercialising any cultural product.

Australia has a long history of multicultural foods starting off as operated and owned by independent families or from ethnic backgrounds, and then becoming cool … [and] too homogenised and commercialised.

She is concerned social media algorithms may also limit access to foods and businesses to those who are already searching for them.

"Opportunities we had before [may have] extended that knowledge and awareness to other communities as well."

Selling food and posting recipes on social media may help provide access to food that is not commonly available — especially to younger generations — but Khorana points out that platforms like Instagram rely heavily on visual aesthetics.

"Not all ethnic food is going to be visually appealing."

Supski acknowledges concerns around the reliance on social media but says it appears to have played a positive role for some people amid concerns about what some say is a loneliness epidemic.

These online communities … bring a lot of connection and support to the people who are selling the food.

title: Flydubai co-pilot used axe in attempted 'terrorist attack', senior UAE official says
text:
IN BRIEF The United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said a recent flydubai incident was an attempted "terrorist attack".

The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi also said.

This article contains references to suicide.

The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel, attempted to carry out a "terrorist attack" during the flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to the state news agency WAM.

The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.

A second source briefed on the investigation confirmed the co-pilot’s name. UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity.

While Emirati authorities have not publicly identified the co-pilot, Israeli officials have previously said he is an Omani national. Oman has not commented on the incident.

"Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack," WAM quoted UAE attorney-general Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying.

The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft, the prosecutor general said.

A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies such as crashes.

Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.

The UAE is leading the investigation. The airline is owned by Dubai's government.

The UAE prosecutor general's comments were the first by Emirati authorities to describe the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.

Disaster was averted on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had attacked the captain in what Israeli officials said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying more than 170 passengers and crew.

A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

The captain and co-pilot left Saudi Arabia for Abu Dhabi on Thursday morning after receiving medical clearance, the Saudi Interior Ministry said.

Flydubai said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and that it was not in a position to comment further, a spokesperson said.

A source briefed on the investigation told Reuters on Friday that Israeli officials were expected to question the co-pilot in the UAE. The source declined to say which Israeli agency or authority would take part.

An Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would take part alongside Emirati authorities in the UAE-led investigation, seeking to determine what happened and examine the suspect's motives and background.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a "heavy price".

Netanyahu said on Thursday that the co-pilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination, without providing details, and appeared suicidal, though he said a motive had not yet been established.

The aircraft dropped about 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the UAE to Israel, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24.

The route is popular among Israeli travellers and most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals.

title: The common viral infections that are responsible for one in eight cancers
text:
in brief A new global analysis has revealed that 12 per cent of cancer is caused by pathogenic infection.

Just four viruses and one bacteria are responsible, opening new pathways for cancer prevention.

Roughly one in every eight cancer cases diagnosed worldwide is triggered by common viral and bacterial infections, rather than inherited genetics or lifestyle factors.

A major global analysis by the World Health Organization body, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, has found that an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 were directly caused by 12 carcinogenic pathogens.

While developing cancer is often viewed as unpredictable, the findings highlight the fact that millions of cases worldwide come from transmissible infections — which are largely preventable.

In an analysis for The Conversation, Dr John La Marca and Dr Sarah Diepstraten, senior research officers at Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, noted that the vast majority of these cancer diagnoses are driven by just a handful of pathogens.

"Four viruses and one bacteria were responsible for 12% of the world's cancer cases in 2024," they wrote.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Kate Broun, deputy chair of Cancer Council’s Cancer Screening and Immunisation Committee, told SBS News that vaccinations and screenings can reduce the risk of cancers.

How does an infection cause cancer?

Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow out of control instead of dying, and is one of the leading causes of death worldwide.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare estimates that around 170,000 new cases of cancer are diagnosed each year in Australia. Roughly 40 per cent of the population will receive a cancer diagnosis by the age of 85.

The disease is caused when normal cell functions are disrupted, something that a virus or a bacterium can trigger.

Certain viruses, like human papillomavirus (HPV), insert their own genetic material directly into human DNA, hijacking cells and deactivating tumour-suppressing proteins. This allows the cells to divide uncontrollably.

"HPV can cause several cancers and other diseases in people of all genders," Broun said. "It is responsible for cases of cervical cancer, anal cancer, vaginal cancer, vulvar cancer, and penile cancer."

Other pathogens, like Helicobacter pylori in the stomach or hepatitis B and C in the liver, operate through persistent, chronic inflammation.

Decades of continuous tissue damage, cell death, and forced regeneration significantly increase the probability of copying errors, which eventually turn healthy cells malignant.

Others still, like HIV, weaken the immune system's natural surveillance mechanisms, which gives other, dormant viruses in the body the chance to activate and trigger tumours.

Which viruses cause cancer?

The report, published in Lancet Oncology, found that four primary pathogens were responsible for the vast majority of infection-driven cancers in 2024.

They were:

H. pylori: A common stomach bacterium responsible for 760,000 cases annually, mainly non-cardia gastric cancers.

HPV: Responsible for 750,000 cases, with cervical cancer making up 600,000 of those diagnoses.

Hepatitis B and C: Driven by chronic liver infections, these caused 360,000 and 160,000 cases of liver cancer, respectively.

Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV): The virus responsible for glandular fever also drove 260,000 cases, with more research needed into its role in throat and stomach cancers, as well as various lymphomas.

Despite being the primary cause behind a substantial number of cancer cases, public awareness of the role pathogens play in the disease is limited.

La Marca and Diepstraten attribute this to the fact that many people carry these pathogens without knowing it.

"These infections can cause more than 20 different types of cancer, including stomach, liver, blood and cervical cancers," they wrote, noting that there is a long delay between infection and cancer onset, which blurs the link.

Preventing future cancer diagnoses

Despite the considerable global figures, researchers emphasise that infection-driven cancers represent the most preventable type on the planet.

Several successful public health interventions for many of these primary pathogens already exist.

HPV and hepatitis B immunisations offer anti-cancer protective properties, while hepatitis C antivirals and antibiotic treatment for H. pylori can eliminate chronic risks before issues develop.

"The HPV vaccine is safe and effective at protecting against HPV-related cancers and diseases," Broun said. "It is recommended and free for Australians aged 12 to 25 years of age."

"Even if you’re vaccinated against HPV, we encourage you to screen."

She added that people uncertain if they have been vaccinated against hepatitis B can speak with their GP about a blood test.

While there is no preventative vaccine against EBV, clinical trials are underway.

"Because these infections are largely preventable or treatable," La Marca and Diepstraten wrote, "scaling up global access to existing vaccines, screening, and antimicrobial therapies offers one of our most direct routes to cutting global cancer rates".

title: 'Adventurous' escaped capybara stays one step ahead after six months on the lam
text:
IN BRIEF Samba escaped with her sister Tango in March while being held in a temporary enclosure.

Zoo staff have been searching for the capybara for six months, responding to over 150 reported sightings.

Samba the capybara has been on the run for six months after escaping a temporary enclosure at Marwell Zoo in the UK.

Samba arrived at Marwell Zoo in Hampshire County on March 16 with her sister, Tango.

The pair were transferred from Jimmy's Farm and Wildlife Park in Suffolk.

Samba and Tango underwent "routine health checks" while their enclosure was being prepared, Marwell Zoo said in a statement.

The following day, while locked in a temporary holding area, the pair attempted a jailbreak.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Samba and Tango had other ideas ... and managed to escape from their new home," the zoo said.

Staff "quickly retrieved" Tango on zoo grounds. But nine-month-old Samba was "more adventurous" and has now been missing for six months.

The first sighting of Samba came a day after her escape in Owslebury, three kilometres from the zoo.

On 22 March, a dog walker spotted Samba lying in the sun on the banks of the River Itchen in the Colden Common area. Startled by the dog walker, Samba scurried down the banks and jumped into the river, making her escape by water.

She was spotted by the river the very next day.

Search efforts increased around the river, but the capybara's excellent camouflage secured her freedom.

Camera traps were placed in various locations where Samba had been spotted, including Twyford, North Twyford, Highbridge and Bambridge Gardens.

Rescue teams also conducted daily ground searches and thermal drone imaging searches — teams responded to 150 reported sightings.

Zoo insists new male not replacing Samba

On 7 July, Marwell Zoo introduced a new capybara.

Seven-year-old male Ripple was transferred from Blackpool Zoo and gradually introduced to the enclosure with Tango.

"His move is first and foremost about ensuring Tango's continued welfare by providing her with appropriate companionship," Marwell Zoo said.

The introduction of the new capybara raised concerns for Samba's future, but the zoo ensured she was not being replaced.

Ripple, a seven-year-old male capybara, has been introduced to Marwell Zoo as a companion animal for Tango, who was experiencing isolation stress. Source: Getty / Mark Metcalfe

"Welcoming Ripple does not mean we have stopped searching for her," they said.

"Our efforts to find Samba continue, and her welfare remains a priority for the team."

The last known sighting of Samba was on 11 August, near Bambridge Gardens.

Marwell Zoo said its team was "acting on a very promising lead" from photographic evidence of the now year-old capybara.

What are capybaras?

Native to South America, capybaras are the world's largest living rodent. They belong to the Caviidae family and are close relatives of the guinea pig and rock cavy.

They can live anywhere between four and eight years in the wild, and 12 in captivity.

Capybaras are semiaquatic herbivores, meaning they can live across savannas and dense forests and near and in freshwater.

They spend most of their time grazing or swimming and are highly social animals, preferring to live in large, close-knit groups of 10 to 40.

The average capybara weighs between 35 and 70 kilograms and stands about 60 centimetres tall.

Usually a slow and calm rodent, capybaras can have bursts of energy. They can reach speeds of 35km/hour when startled or threatened.

This speed helps them escape predators or, apparently, zookeepers eager to return them to captivity.

title: How daylight saving leaves one Australian border town operating on two different clocks
text:
In brief Daylight saving returns this weekend, renewing calls for southeast Queensland to adopt the time change.

Border businesses near Tweed Heads and Coolangatta are preparing for booking mix-ups and confusion.

Same headache, new year.

In the wee hours of Sunday morning, daylight saving kicks in for the long Australian summer, when clocks skip forward by an hour from 2am to 3am.

But while the citizens of NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and the ACT will enjoy an extra hour of sunshine after clocking off, Queensland remains the eastern seaboard outlier.

Daylight saving is an annual talking point on the Gold Coast, with Mayor Tom Tate on Wednesday reiterating calls for daylight saving to be introduced in Queensland's southeast corner.

Tate suggested drawing a new time zone boundary north of Noosa — cheekily acknowledging the lack of support elsewhere from cows and the wider dairy industry.

But for businesses in the NSW border town of Tweed Heads, as well as Coolangatta on the Queensland side, the issue is no joke.

Ellen Clark, a cosmetic nurse, recently opened a business in Tweed Heads and is bracing herself for late arrivals from her clientele, most of whom are in Queensland.

"It's going to be interesting trying to navigate that," she told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).

Previously, Ms Clark commuted to Brisbane for work from Tweed Heads, where her partner is based, but decided to set up shop locally after the birth of her first child.

"I used to have to stay on Queensland time while my partner would operate on NSW time," she said.

"It kind of came to my attention yesterday, and I was like, 'Oh my God, we're back here again'."

Sean McMillan is also new to Tweed Heads, having just set up a barber shop on Bay Street.

"All my systems go off bookings, so I'm trying to do some research, and I'm changing my hours a little bit to catch people on both sides of the border," he told the AAP.

"I'm sure there'll be people coming in an hour early or an hour late for bookings ... It's just one of those puzzles to work out."

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli was not keen to buy into Tate's suggestion when asked about the issue by reporters in Mackay on Thursday.

"I've lived at both ends of the state, and I'm here for uniting Queensland, not dividing it," he said.

Queensland trialled daylight saving between 1989 and 1992 before being comprehensively rejected in a state referendum.

Plans to replace an older unit block with an $85 million luxury apartment complex on Oxford Street in Paddington have been approved by the Minns government despite concerns from hundreds of residents, the local MP and Woollahra Council that it would result in fewer relatively affordable homes. Citing the delivery of more than 40 well-located dwellings, the state government approved developer Toohey Miller’s proposal to bulldoze a three-storey block of 27 studio apartments and several townhouses for an eight-storey building of 44 units opposite the Victoria Barracks military base in Sydney’s east. The eight-storey block that Sydney developer Toohey Miller is proposing includes double-storey penthouses. Smart Design Studio Eleven of the new units will be affordable housing offered at below-market rent for 15 years, which triggered criticism the development would lead to an overall loss of moderately priced homes. Independent Woollahra councillor Harriet Price, who represents the Paddington ward, said tenants at the 50-year-old apartment block approved for demolition had last week “[woken] to the sound of a large truck delivering building materials and hoardings to the development site”.

The bulk of 377 public submissions the government received on the proposal were negative. Of the 332 objections, 80 per cent raised concerns the building would be at odds with Paddington’s character, while 69 per cent were worried about the loss of low-cost or affordable housing. Woollahra Council objected to the net loss of affordable dwellings and lack of smaller apartments; the height, bulk and scale of the “incompatible” building; traffic congestion and negative impacts on the Paddington heritage conservation area and Victoria Barracks. The existing apartment block on Oxford Street, opposite Victoria Barracks. The Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure recommended the project for approval subject to conditions. Its assessment report said the block’s bulk and scale aligned with state planning controls for the site, would not have unreasonable privacy or overshadowing impacts, was compatible with the desired future character of the area, and would not adversely impact heritage.

There is a point in any negotiation when resolve begins to look like stubbornness. When holding firm ceases to be a demonstration of strength and instead becomes an exercise in proving that strength exists. Essendon are approaching that point with Zach Merrett. Essendon president Andrew Welsh. Getty Images The former skipper wants to leave (again). Hawthorn want him (again). Essendon know it. Everyone in football knows it. At some point the Bombers need to stop trying to win the negotiation and start trying to win again. There is a difference. The Bombers have spent too much of the past two decades fighting battles that ultimately haven’t taken them anywhere. They have changed coaches, chief executives, presidents, football bosses and strategies. They have defended their people, sacked their people, promised patience and demanded standards. Still, the drought goes on. But now they have a choice. They can spend another trade period arguing over precisely what a 31-year-old Merrett is worth, extracting every last drop from Hawthorn and telling the football world they will not be pushed around.

Advertisement

Or they can make the deal, take the picks and move forward. Hawthorn’s opening offer this year, of picks 15 and 25 and a future third-round selection, was rejected. Fine. It was an opening bid. Essendon are entitled to ask for more and Hawthorn should expect to pay a premium for a contracted champion. Merrett requested a move to the Hawks in 2025 but was unsuccessful. Getty Images But this cannot become another exercise in institutional pride. Merrett has given Essendon more than enough.

Advertisement

He has won seven Crichton medals. He has carried the club through some of the bleakest years in its history. He stayed when leaving would have been understandable. He performed while administrations changed around him and September success remained perpetually on the horizon. Now, at 31, he wants the opportunity to chase something Essendon have been unable to give him: a premiership. Holding him to his contract might be Essendon’s right. That doesn’t make it right for Essendon. And there is an irony here that should not be lost on anyone. More than two decades ago, Essendon and Hawthorn played the famous “Line in the Sand” game.

Advertisement

Perhaps it is time for the Bombers to draw another one. Not with Hawthorn – for themselves. Draw a line underneath the Merrett era. Draw a line underneath the idea that refusing to trade a player somehow proves you are a powerful football club. Draw a line underneath the obsession with winning the argument. Strong clubs don’t need to constantly tell everyone they’re strong. They make hard decisions and live with them.

Advertisement

Related Article Live

AFL 2026 AFL trade period day one: Saints put hefty price tag on ruckman; Pies secure Hogan and farewell Pendlebury Welsh says Hawthorn underestimated Essendon and “where we are going”. Good – then go there. If Essendon genuinely believe in their direction, the departure of one 31-year-old midfielder – even one as decorated and important as Merrett – cannot be allowed to derail it. Take the best deal available. Turn those selections into players who can be part of Essendon’s next serious premiership push. Give the next generation ownership of the football club, and let Merrett go.

Advertisement

That doesn’t mean giving Hawthorn whatever they want. It doesn’t mean rolling over. And it certainly doesn’t mean accepting an inadequate deal simply to make the problem disappear. Negotiate hard, but get a deal done. Because there is a difference between driving a hard bargain and holding a player hostage to make a point. Essendon need to decide what matters more: proving to Hawthorn that they cannot be bullied, or building the football club that Welsh insists is coming. The Bombers don’t need another victory at the trade table. They need victories on the football field. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. title: ‘He’s outstanding’: Why George Gregan has been blown away by an 11-Test Wallabies halfback
text:
Advertisement

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘He’s outstanding’: Why George Gregan has been blown away by an 11-Test Wallabies halfback Iain Payten October 5, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

He only made his Test debut a little over a year ago and has just 11 caps for the Wallabies, but halfback Ryan Lonergan has already impressed great Wallabies No.9 George Gregan so much he views him as one of Australia’s most valuable players, and even likened the Canberra star to iconic South African Fourie Du Preez. Praise for Lonergan also came from another World Cup winning star, with Dan Carter saying his maturity and leadership can help compensate for the Wallabies’ problems at five-eighth. Loading Lonergan has been outstanding for the Wallabies this year, having started in every Test. After enduring a 93-game, nine-season wait for a Test debut, the 28-year-old finally got his shot off the bench at Eden Park last year. Lonergan will be back at the All Blacks’ fortress again this week, but this time he will be wearing the No.9. He grabbed the jumper in July following injuries to Jake Gordon and Tate McDermott and, based on subsequent form, Lonergan won’t be handing it back any time soon.

Advertisement

With a strong passing game, the Brumbies skipper has been instrumental in marshalling the Wallabies’ red zone attack. Lonergan’s kicking game has also been high quality, be it long, contestable or off the tee. The right-footer has kicked 30 of 33 goals since July. Ryan Lonergan takes on the Springboks in Perth. He has become a key player for the Wallabies in a short period of time. Getty Images Lonergan’s 17 points (seven from eight) against the Springboks in Perth was the difference in a game where both sides scored five tries. His only blemish was one of the four yellow cards. “He’s outstanding,” Gregan said. “He’s always had a really good skill set; he’s been a very good player for a number of years. He’s been knocking on the door. The door opened and he’s run through it.

Advertisement

“That performance [against the Springboks] was outstanding. I know Tate is there as well, and that competition’s good. They’re different, they provide different options. “The way Ryan controlled that game on the weekend, it really took a lot of pressure off the 10. Ryan Lonergan makes a break against Japan in Townsville. Getty Images “He really took a lot of responsibility. He can play both sides of the ruck, which I always love. It’s basic, it’s a fundamental. A good nine can scan and play both sides. “And his kicking game, short and long, it’s really balanced. He only missed a goal. It was an unbelievable performance.

Advertisement

“I was on a pod[cast], talking to [former Springbok captain] John Smit … and I said, ‘Mate, there was a glimpse of Fourie Du Preez there.’ It had that kind of look to it, and I don’t think I can give a bigger rap than that.” Du Preez, who starred in the Boks’ 2007 World Cup win, is rated by many Test players as one of the best No.9s of the modern era, along with Gregan. Eddie Jones said it was like having an extra coach on the field when Du Preez was playing. Fourie Du Preez scoring for the Springboks in 2015. Getty Images Despite his lack of experience at Test level, Carter said Lonergan could prove crucial to the Wallabies at the World Cup if they can’t find a consistent No.10. “You want some stability there, but if you’re not going to have an experienced 50 to 100-cap No.10, you’ve got to have a really stable No.9, and a solid midfield partner,” Carter said.

Advertisement

“And they [the Wallabies] have got the talent there. I’ve been really impressed with Ryan Lonergan, and just the way he leads out on the field. He’s been patient, and he’s made the most of his opportunity. He’s been in leadership roles with the Brumbies, so he brings a calmness and a real leadership element. That will help the No.10.” Related Article Analysis

Australian rugby Why the Wallabies should rest their best player for opening Bledisloe at Eden Park Kiss said he knew Lonergan would be an asset. “He’s been superb to coach, and in a lot of ways, I’m not surprised,” Kiss said. “He was a thorn in our side when I was coaching [the Reds]. “He’s a quality player and a quality individual, who does the simple things well. But simple things have a big impact on our game, the way we can play the game.”

Advertisement

Gregan said the key for Lonergan was to carry through one of his strongest traits at the Brumbies to Test level: “It’s just about backing it up and being consistent, and he definitely has that.” Meanwhile, the Australian under-18 side has recorded a fourth straight victory over the New Zealand Schools team with a 40-33 win in Hamilton. Led by rising Waratah flanker Justice Taumoepeau, the Aussie under-18s trailed 19-12 at half-time but powered home in the second half with tries to Hasani Bloomfield, Harrison Asi and reserve halfback Izak Holmes. The young Aussies had impressive performers right across the park, who will be sighted in Super Rugby in the future. Giant lock pair Jack Burton and Asi were strong, and so were back-rowers Tahj Smith and Hunter Reich. Out wide, Wilson Ruthven was excellent in steering a back line featuring impressive centres James Smith and Taione Taka, and elusive fullback Jack Plamondon, who is a star of the future.

title: With one last magic moment, DCE shows he’ll be a Hull of a big loss for the NRL
text:
Advertisement

SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion With one last magic moment, DCE shows he’ll be a Hull of a big loss for the NRL Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist October 5, 2026 — 3:30pm

October 5, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Daly Cherry-Evans kicked 28 field goals in 352 games for Manly, many of them match-winners. To see him do it in a grand final for the Roosters would have evoked mixed feelings for the Sea Eagles, but seriously? He gave so much to Manly, keeping them competitive year after year and week after week, often single-handedly (and double-footedly with those drop-kicks off his left or right), that it’s a bit amnesic to begrudge him the joy of going out a winner. Loading His recruitment, like Cooper Cronk’s in 2018, proved the difference for the Roosters in 2026. Fifteen years apart, Cherry-Evans owned two grand final nights. Hull have got a good one. Are all clubs created equal?

Advertisement

The Roosters will just have to live with the fact that most of the rugby league community don’t believe they, already premiership contenders, were able to recruit Cherry-Evans and Reece Robson and remain under the salary cap. I don’t think they’ll struggle with it. Another premiership trophy offers pretty warm comfort and a high hill to crow from. But in these polarising times, it’s difficult to imagine a grand final with two more divergent potential narratives. The Roosters’ NRL and NRLW teams celebrate their premierships together. Audrey Richardson Newcastle win, from last to first, and it gives every club heart. The Roosters win, and it suggests that the salary cap is not stopping wealthy clubs from hoarding talent. The Roosters’ counter-argument is that Naufahu Whyte, Rob Toia, Sam Walker and many more of its representative stars are one-club players; by which logic, Penrith wouldn’t have had to let go Stephen Crichton, Matt Burton, Jarome Luai, James Fisher-Harris and Viliame Kikau ... The margin might have only been one point in Sunday’s grand final, but the broader fan sentiment is very black and white. Not since David Gallop was chief executive has the NRL responded seriously to concerns about the failure of the cap to help equalise the talent pool.

Advertisement

It’s a bit tough to swallow any “fans first” rhetoric while some clubs remain, like George Orwell’s animals, more equal than others. Bring back the entertainment It’s a rule of every sporting event that there has to be a “random Souths guy”, and on Sunday night, that role fell to Jai Arrow. Retired South Sydney player Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles take part in a lap of honour. Getty Images In all the debate about how appropriate it was to have a sad and sombre moment as pre-grand final “entertainment”, and the inevitable last squeeze of shared sentiment to take it across the line into sentimentality, there wasn’t much about the Souths-ness of the situation.

Advertisement

A 100-game Rabbitoh was the centre of attention on the Roosters’ big night. In terms of tribalism, I’m not sure who was more put off: Souths, for having their man headline a Roosters game, or the Roosters, for having their grand final thunder stolen by someone from their enemy. Of course, Arrow’s diagnosis with motor neurone disease has transcended tribalism and brought rugby league together. But tribalism is more resilient and permanent than individuals, and the best that can be said about Arrow’s lap of honour, accompanied by Nathan Charles (a former rugby player with the same horrible disease), is that the league was making the best of a bad situation. With any luck, it will be a one-off, and the NRL will get its act together sooner about what it organises for its big night. Ali Brigginshaw was emotional after the Brisbane Broncos grand final defeat to the Roosters on Sunday. Getty Images Brigginshaw will always be game’s first champion Ali Brigginshaw, after nine seasons for the Broncos, four premierships, 13 Origins for

Queensland and 29 Tests for Australia, retired after the NRLW grand final with a legacy as the foundation stone of women’s rugby league in this country.

Advertisement

She is to the sport what Betty Wilson was to women’s cricket and Fanny Durack was to women’s swimming. As that first great champion, she can never be superseded. Brigginshaw’s final act as a player was to get whacked in the head as she completed a tough offload, still on the attack, looking for points even after Brisbane were well beaten. What a career. The game will always owe her. Great Dane was a Kiwi all along Having watched Dane Gagai torment NSW in 23 Origin matches for a decade, I’m sure I’m not the only one who thought he was a Queenslander. Seven Kangaroos Test appearances confirmed he was Australian. But it turns out he’s a New Zealander.

Advertisement

In a convoluted judgment wrapped up in the cover-all “special circumstances”, Gagai has been granted his request to represent the Kiwis in the upcoming World Cup. Related Article Opinion

NRL grand final Despite heartbreaking result, Knights remain the people’s choice Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author At 35, he is following his Newcastle teammate Kalyn Ponga in dissolving the old rule that players could not switch their representation between “tier one” nations. Now, we all know that international rugby league has been turned into a thing by the steady decanting of what would previously have been Australian players through other nations. It’s smart business and is going to make the World Cup as credible as it can possibly be. That said, New Zealand don’t need Australian defectors – they are good enough to win on their own. In the Indian summer that Gagai’s career is enjoying, it would surprise no one to see him emerge next month with a winner’s medal in black and white.

San Francisco: A researcher in Siberia has reportedly died of a disease suspected to be a form of plague released by a laboratory accident. Russian authorities are responding to the incident at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East in Shelekhov, a city just west of Irkutsk near the border with Mongolia, according to state media. The Siberian institute studies “especially dangerous infectious diseases”, relating to surveillance, treatment and biological safety, according to its website. Getty Images Although it remains unclear what was released, a 28-year-old woman who worked in a laboratory at the institute died after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of unknown origin, according to Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s infectious disease agency. “The sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is stable,” the agency said in a statement to CNN.

Advertisement

It said exceptional measures had been taken “in connection with the case of an employee of the Irkutsk Antiplague Institute”. The institute studies “especially dangerous infectious diseases”, relating to surveillance, treatment and biological safety, according to its website. Citing information from Rospotrebnadzor, Alexei Tsydenov, the head of the neighbouring republic of Buryatia, said the woman “may have died of plague”, but that there were “no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in the areas bordering Mongolia”. Tsydenov did not specify the type of plague, but Russian media have reported that the disease was pneumonic plague, the only form that can be spread from person to person.

Advertisement

The woman, identified by Russian media as Daria Sh., reportedly told medical staff she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria while collecting samples. She was taken to hospital in Shelekhov last Tuesday with symptoms of severe pneumonia and placed on a ventilator before dying two days later, according to the Moscow Times. All public events in Irkutsk have been cancelled, and Russian media have reported that law enforcement has opened a criminal investigation into possible safety violations surrounding the woman’s death. iStock Reports in Russian media state that about 200 people at the hospital where the worker was taken were placed under observation, and a quarantine was imposed at a maternity hospital. Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, said an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission had been called with Russia’s chief state doctor, “prompted by reports of a suspected case of a highly dangerous infectious disease in a regional resident”.

Advertisement

Kobzev urged calm, writing on Telegram that none of the contacts of the dead woman were showing any signs of illness and all testing had come back negative. Gennady Onishchenko, a former head of Rospotrebnadzor, said on Friday that the infection was “most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease”. Irkutsk Region Governor Igor Kobzev, pictured with Russian President Vladimir Putin last year, said an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission had been called with Russia’s chief state doctor. AP CNN reported that an aluminium plant near the laboratory had ordered workers to wear masks as a precaution, but noted there were “many rumours and conflicting reports circulating”, said Artem Fominikh, the plant’s director. All public events in Irkutsk have been cancelled, and Russian media have reported that law enforcement has opened a criminal investigation into possible safety violations surrounding the woman’s death.

Advertisement

Pneumonic plague, one of three types of the disease caused by theYersinia pestis bacterium, is the most serious form of plague. It develops when a person inhales infectious droplets or when bacteria from untreated septicaemic or bubonic plague, which caused the Black Death, spread to the lungs of an infected person. A Trump administration official told news website Axios that the White House was monitoring reports of the disease and quarantines. text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Critical brings gold guns to Suriname hunt Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 5, 2026 — 3:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Critical Resources has engaged a firm of exploration specialists with extensive on-the-ground experience to kick off a hunt for the structural keys to its gold projects in Suriname, South America. The company recently secured exclusivity over the Gonini and Greenstars projects in September, which sit in the Guiana Shield - a vast, ancient geological region in northern South America, stretching across Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and parts of Venezuela and Brazil. Its old greenstone belts host major gold deposits and are geologically related to West Africa’s prolific Birimian gold belts, which were joined to the Guiana Shield before the Atlantic Ocean opened. Critical Resources’ Gonini and Greenstars gold projects sit in Suriname’s Guiana Shield, a region known for major gold deposits. Subject to the deals completing, the ASX-listed junior will hold a 90 per cent interest in 199 square kilometres of granted gold exploitation rights. Critical has now brought in experts GexplOre to run a major structural and geophysical interpretation across Gonini and Greenstars, in addition to more than 6000 square kilometres of the surrounding greenstone belt. The savvy move marks a significant step for Critical, which says it is the first ASX-listed company in decades to explore for gold in the country.

Advertisement

‘Engaging them now means we can build our structural picture and help us screen further opportunities across the belt.’ Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither GexplOre is no stranger to the Guiana Shield, having worked on about 20 gold projects across Suriname, Guyana and French Guiana. Notably, the firm has provided structural work for G Mining Ventures’ impressive Oko West project in Guyana and Founders Metals’ Antino project in Suriname, a project that has seen Canadian major Gold Fields tip in C$77 (A$77.7) million for a 19.9 per cent stake. Critical’s study will be a two-stage affair. The first stage involves a detailed, property-scale interpretation over two priority target areas at the 164-square-kilometre Gonini project. The second is a lower-resolution review of the wider greenstone belt, designed to screen for further opportunities. The work will process satellite elevation and spectral data, tapping into Gexplore’s existing database, to map host rocks, shear and fault corridors, and folding events that are known to control gold mineralisation in the region. In a deeply weathered and forest-covered terrain where rock outcrop is scarce, a satellite-based structural study is a logical and low-cost first filter to identify settings that might host gold before committing to more expensive on-ground work.

Advertisement

The wider Guiana Shield is considered hot property for gold exploration, with recent coverage highlighting it as significantly underexplored while attracting fresh capital. The region’s gold sector is already a major economic driver for Suriname, with the United States Geological Survey noting gold production delivered US$2 billion (A$2.9B) in export revenue in 2024 and accounted for 79 per cent of the country’s total exports. Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “The Gonini and Greenstars projects give ASX investors a rare opportunity for exposure to the Guiana Shield greenstone belt in Suriname, and give us the opportunity to continue to grow our footprint within Suriname and the greater Guiana Shield. Gexplore brings structural experience from some of the most significant discoveries in the Shield, including G Mining Ventures’ Oko West in Guyana and Founders Metals’ Antino in Suriname.” The company’s ground sits within the same Marowijne greenstone belt that hosts Newmont’s 5.1-million-ounce Merian mine, 66km away and Zijin Mining’s Rosebel mine, some 88km away. Rosebel has been in production since 2004, producing 5.65 million ounces of gold between 2004 and 2021 before Zijin acquired it from IAMGOLD for US$360 (A$518) million in 2023. While both of Critical’s projects have a long history of small-scale mining, there is little to no record of modern systematic exploration. Legal, title and technical due diligence on both projects is being fast-tracked, with site visits and in-country introductions slated for the coming weeks, allowing the company to quickly start exploration once the acquisition conditions are satisfied. Elsewhere, the company continues to roll out its Mavis Lake lithium project in Canada, home to an eight-million- tonne resource at 1.07 per cent lithium oxide. It also holds an option over intellectual property for solid-state battery technology and has licensed thermal management tech targeting AI high-density electronics data centres.

Advertisement

Additionally, Critical holds the Halls Peak base metals project in New South Wales featuring an inferred resource of 840,000 tonnes at 3.7 per cent zinc, 1.5 per cent lead and 0.44 per cent copper alongside a growing portfolio of gold, antimony and tungsten prospects across a 1694-square-kilometre ground package in New Zealand. With legal and technical due diligence on the acquisitions ongoing, the structural study will serve to give Critical a running start. By building a structural framework now, the company hopes a first boot-on-ground campaign can head straight to the highest-ranked ground once the deals are finalised, allowing exploration to kick off at full tilt.
