title: Inside the building of a Boeing 737 – from scratch
text:
Advertisement

BusinessCompaniesAviation Inside the building of a Boeing 737 – from scratch Chris Zappone October 5, 2026 — 3:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Few aircraft are more closely watched than the Boeing 737. Since first rolling off the assembly line in 1967, it has been in continuous production, and more than 12,000 airframes have been sold. In the process, it has created a legacy that has defined modern air travel, shaping how airports are built and the business models of airlines. There are 10 main stages to the production of a Boeing 737. Chris Zappone Boeing 737s are everywhere in global aviation – comprising whole fleets in some cases, and making up the backbones of others, such as those of Qantas and Virgin’s domestic operations. In recent years, however, the world’s most important commercial airliner has received attention for another, troubling, reason. The 737 has been tainted by design defects and quality control failures, most notably highlighted by the tragic crashes of two 737 MAX 8 jets in 2018 and 2019, which led to a worldwide grounding and direct US Federal Aviation Administration production oversight.

Advertisement

Loading The aviation icon now sits at the centre of a crisis of trust, but is, in a way, a symbol of American – and even Western – manufacturing. The symbolism is underpinned by commercial realities. The other pressing reason the 737 gets so much attention is that the world’s airlines remain hungry for new, more efficient 737 MAX airframes. The MAX uses 20 per cent less fuel than previous versions of the 737. Boeing says the MAX line offers airlines greater profit potential and it averages 7 per cent lower operating costs with up to 14 per cent lower maintenance costs than its competitor. This masthead recently secured access to a Boeing factory (after lengthy negotiations with the company) in Renton, Washington state. The facility has been the home of 737 production since 1970. Ten ‘flow days’

Advertisement

The 737 begins life as the fuselage, shipped in by train from Kansas, where it’s made, and enters the factory. Fuselages arrive by rail, in the distinct green colour of their protective primer. From there, each fuselage is rolled and lifted into position in an elevated part of the factory, where it is inspected. Insulation, electronic, hydraulic, and mechanical parts are then installed. Fuselages fresh in by train from Kansas at Boeing’s Renton, Washington state, factory. Chris Zappone At this point, the fuselages are lined up closely three abreast as they undergo their first three “flow days” – a term for the station of production. It takes 10 flow days, with each day representing a specific stop along the assembly line for the fuselage – to put a 737 together. The first three comprise wiring (about 70 kilometres’ worth), and putting in hydraulic tubing, flight control cables, the dorsal fin, and the controls within the flight deck. A protective cover for the radar at the tip of the plane’s nose is also installed in this phase.

Advertisement

In somewhat confusing nomenclature, the flow days are usually longer than 24 hours. The pacing of production is designed with enough of a gap to allow for minor delays or unexpected changes. On day four, the fuselages are moved down from the upper level of the factory onto the floor. To get them into lines, a crane mounted in the ceiling of the enormous facility moves them through a special gap in the wall into three parallel floor assembly lines. A busy but orderly floor at Boeing’s Renton factory. Chris Zappone Here the fuselages are spread out nose to tail. The three floor assembly lines are called the West Line, the Central Line and the East Line. This year Boeing opened a North Line for 737 production. Based in Everett, Washington, the North Line will expand Boeing’s capacity to build 737 MAX-family jets to meet market demand, including a current order backlog of 4300.

Advertisement

In the Renton factory, movement by crane happens at night, and it takes about an hour per fuselage. The factory runs 24 hours a day year-round except Christmas and the Thanksgiving holiday in late November. Boeing 737s have been made at the factory for decades. Chris Zappone Compared with Airbus factories, Boeing’s shop floor is more densely filled with equipment, and seems more like a factory. Staff call out to each other over the machine sounds of production. Workstations where specialised tasks and technical problem-solving take place are positioned along the floor. Between the buildings, staff move on shuttles, cars and scooters. The train line bringing the fuselages from Kansas comes right through the campus. Flow day four is always the big one for the 737. This is when it gets its wings, horizontal and vertical stabilisers, and landing gear. (The winglets, or tips of wings that flare up and down, are primarily made at Boeing’s Melbourne facility in Fishermans Bend.)

Advertisement

From there, the plane can rest on its own weight and is ready for the next step, in which the toilets, galleys and water and wastewater tanks are installed. The side walls, overhead bins and forward galleys are installed the day after. Carpeting and seats come on day eight. Boeing installs the seats using a machine similar to a hay baler, or an inclined conveyor belt that takes the seats up three at a time into the door, where technicians receive them and install them in the plane. Despite delays in cabin seat availability and FAA certification in wide-body planes, seats for the 737 have had less complexity, and hence, fewer hold-ups. On day nine, the engines are installed and connected to the electronic and hydraulic systems. The factory floor. Chris Zappone

Advertisement

All up, it takes 15 days from the fuselage coming into the factory to the plane being completed and made ready for inspection by the purchasing airline. After that, test flights are conducted over central Washington state. Factory employees lunch within view of the planes in progress, either eating at canteens or bringing their own food, and sitting at lunch tables on the balcony overlooking the main action. The vast building also houses offices, which gives it a hive-like feeling. One Boeing employee said working in the office in this building was more fun simply because he could look out and see the planes being put together at scale. Britain is considering imposing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicle imports amid concerns that Beijing is flooding the market with state-subsidised cars, The Times newspaper reported on Sunday. Business minister Jonathan Reynolds is drawing up a package of potential tariffs on Chinese vehicle imports, the report said, citing concerns that Chinese manufacturers are “dumping” subsidised vehicles into Britain. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Chinese EV maker BYD’s electrical vehicles attract 100 per cent tariffs upon entry to the US. Getty Asked to comment, a spokesperson from the British government told Reuters no tariffs have been imposed on Chinese EVs. “We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests,” the spokesperson said in an email.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Energy Fuel giant Ampol zooms past Tesla as Australia’s top EV charger owner British ministers are ready to match the European Union’s 45 per cent levy on Chinese electric cars, The Times said, to avoid the pain of “Made in Europe” proposals, which could impact UK companies selling into the EU. The EU’s “Made in Europe” policy is aimed at reducing reliance on Chinese components by prioritising European-made goods, raising concerns among British automakers that supply parts into European manufacturing chains and sell vehicles across the bloc. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he would make the case that Britain should be treated as a “trusted partner” under the proposed EU rules, warning that excluding the UK could damage its car industry. The Financial Times reported in September that Brussels had urged Burnham to align more closely with EU trade policy and raise tariffs on Chinese cars if Britain wants to avoid the “Made in Europe” barriers.

Advertisement

According to The Times, citing senior government sources, ministers believe any decision on tariffs should be based on Britain’s national interest rather than automatically following the EU’s lead. Meanwhile, the outlook for EVs is starting to brighten after the slump last year in the US market after Republican-backed legislation signed by US President Donald Trump eliminated the federal government’s $US7500 EV tax credit a year ago. The looming cancellation triggered a brief surge in sales, pushing EV market share to an all-time high of nearly 11 per cent in last year’s third quarter. However, the inevitable decline that followed left dealers with a glut of unsold EVs and many auto executives searching for a natural level of US demand for EVs, without help from subsidies. That is beginning to come into clearer view. Elon Musk’s Tesla and its rival, Rivian Automotive, have both posted better-than-expected EV sales for the third quarter.

Related Article Electric vehicles One EV sold every 100 seconds: More electric cars to hit Australia’s roads Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles worldwide in the period, according to the company. That compared with 463,761 expected on average among analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg. The results are encouraging for Tesla following a period of declining auto sales and a lagging stock price. With competition in the crucial China market and sluggish demand in the US pressuring the company, Musk is working to reorient Tesla around the futuristic business lines of artificial intelligence, driverless vehicles and humanoid robots. “The deliveries figure is impressive,” Tom Narayan, an analyst with RBC Capital Markets, said in a note. Tesla is probably benefiting from a pullback by large US automakers from the EV market, he said, as well as high fuel costs that are driving demand for electric vehicles.

Elsewhere, executives at Hyundai Motor and Ford Motor have also flagged that dealers are asking for more battery-powered inventory to sell as customers come back. Even some lower-volume models from Toyota and General Motor’s Cadillac brand are gaining momentum. The key driver for renewed customer uptake has been the war in Iran pushing up petrol and diesel prices. “Because of the war, because of gas prices, we’ve also seen a rise and a recovery in EV sales,” said Randy Parker, chief executive officer of Hyundai’s North America business. “I’ve got more and more dealers now asking for EV product.” In Australia, a record 157,958 electric vehicles were sold in the six months to June, more than double the number of sales during the same period a year earlier, according to the Electric Vehicle Council’s latest annual figures, released in September. Fully battery-electric vehicles accounted for 103,716 of those sales, while the remaining 54,241 were plug-in hybrids. With an electric vehicle sold every 100 seconds in Australia during the first half of this calendar year, electric vehicles have expanded their share of Australia’s new car market from 10 per cent last year to more than 25 per cent – or one in four new cars sold – as of last month. Works have begun on the renewal of one of Western Australia’s oldest working pieces of infrastructure – the Perth to Kalgoorlie water pipeline. About 44.5 kilometres of the 566 kilometre-long pipeline, designed by famed WA engineer CY O’Connor, will be replaced to boost the amount of water able to be pumped through it by 10 per cent. Goldfields CY O’Connor water pipeline. The $543 million project also includes doubling the Binduli Reservoir capacity from 400 million litres to 800 million litres. The demand for water in the Goldfields has increased by 16 per cent in the past five years, and Kalgoorlie’s mining industry is currently hampered by its lack of commercial water supply, with the existing pipeline for drinking water only.

Advertisement

Most businesses draw water from the ground, which is six times as salty as seawater. WA Water Minister Daniel Pastorelli said, from 2027, an additional 7.2 million litres would flow into the Goldfields every day. “The Goldfields pipeline is one of the most important pieces of economic infrastructure in the state’s history,” he said. “It served the Goldfields and the Wheatbelt for now 120 years, providing water to a whole vast range of different communities and industries, and supported economic development for many, many years. “Today marks the beginning of the next chapter.”

Advertisement

The new section of the pipeline runs through the shires of Westonia, Merredin, and Yilgarn, and much of it will be buried. Related Article Gold Super Pit owner Northern Star knocks back $39B takeover bid “The pipelines are being manufactured and delivered locally, and will last up to 150 years,” Pastorelli said. The pipeline was the brainchild of WA’s first engineer-in-chief, Charles Yelverton (CY) O’Connor. Work began in the late 1890s after the first gold was discovered in what is now the (aptly named) Goldfields.

Advertisement

The pipeline was completed in 1903, but, famously, O’Connor never got to see water pumping through it because he killed himself at South Beach in Fremantle three weeks before the first pump station began operating amid a royal commission into the project. Premier Roger Cook flagged this project was the first of more stages yet to be announced. The Cook government has previously raised pumping desalinated water from Esperence into the Goldfields as another solution to the region’s water woes. On Monday, Cook said that idea had been probed, but it was decided upgrading the existing Perth pipeline was a better investment. However, he noted Esperence would need a desalination plant at some point. “We will need desalination plants that link and breadth of this state, both as part of a growing economy but also a drying planet,” he said.

Advertisement

“Whether you ultimately see a desalination plant in Esperance feeding the Goldfields region more generally, or simply meeting the needs of the growing Esperance community, I think you will need desal there.” Kalgoorlie Mayor Glenn Wilson welcomed the start of works. “If it wasn’t for water here in Kalgoorlie-Boulder, we wouldn’t be here,” he said. “We welcome, after many years of not having a lot of maintenance or love spent on a pipeline, we’ve got it now and it’s happening.”

★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview TV’s most fascinating experiment ends with an emotional gut-punch Paul Kalina Updated October 5, 2026 — 3:10pm ,first published October 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

70 Up ★★★★ 70 Up brings to a close one of the most fascinating – and arguably the longest-running – shows in the annals of TV history. It started in 1964 with a group of 14 children from a cross-section of English society in the documentary Seven Up! It was there we met Cockney lad Tony, who at age seven planned to be a jockey; headstrong Jackie, who said she would marry a boy with money; and Paul, who was raised in a boy’s home and in reply to a question about his future education replied, “What’s a university?” Every seven years since, director and behind-the-camera interviewer Michael Apted returned to see how these playful children became feisty teenagers, then parents and eventually grandparents; how marriages were made and unmade; how hopes soared and were sometimes extinguished. John, Bruce, Symon, Andrew, Suzy, Jackie, Tony, Sue, Peter, Paul and Neil all return for 70 Up, reportedly the final instalment of this famous documentary series. ITV The original concept was to test the Jesuit adage, “Give me a child until he is seven and I will give you the man” – a window into how class and socioeconomic circumstances determine the chances and opportunities that shape their (and our own) lives. But what it’s mostly remembered for today is the front-row seat it offered to the daily dramas of life and how each of the participants was forged into the person that they became.

Advertisement

Now, here they are as 70-year-olds looking back, but also forwards, in what is touted to be the last instalment of the show. Related Article Review 63 Up's Aussie battler Paul Kligerman on the call he dreads every seven years In the two-part 70 Up, we see where the 13 surviving people have ended up (Lynn, the librarian, died in 2013). For the most part, they’re fulfilled, contented and self-aware – which may be surprising given the challenges some have faced. They are also deeply contemplative and ruminative, not only about how their lives have unfolded but how they’ve been depicted in the films. Directed by Asif Kapadia (Amy, Senna, Diego Maradona), 70 Up is very much about legacy (Apted died in 2021). At stake is not only the personal legacies of the participants, but the legacy of the series itself. Several talk about how the show has turned them into celebrities, and we are poignantly reminded that as seven-year-olds they never really consented to be part of a program that has come to define them. They all return, however, for this last hurrah – even some who opted not to participate in earlier instalments. Their humility and, ultimately, gratitude are truly heartrending.

Advertisement

Sue and Claire reflect on their past selves. SBS/ITV Indeed, 70 Up raises many valid questions about Apted’s agendas and preconceived ideas, such as the sexist questions he put to the female participants, as well as setting up the posh schoolboys to look like undeserving twits. “Sneering and supercilious” is how one of the participants remembers him. Hearing some of Apted’s loaded and insulting questions from earlier chapters is cringe-making. Editor's pick Australian TV ‘That’s got to count for something’: Julia Morris and Julia Zemiro on four decades in the spotlight That’s one part of the legacy that 70 Up wants to correct. The other is that the series’ focus on outdated notions of class and society meant it wasn’t always asking the right questions. It’s here that 70 Up, its second episode in particular, delivers an emotional punch to the gut. There’s Neil, the sunny daydreamer in Seven Up! who now talks with admirable candour about his lifelong mental health battles. And Symon, who still rues having never met his father, and has gone on to foster more than 100 children. What we take away isn’t the fairness of the cards they were dealt but how they faced the unpredictable twists and turns that life put in their paths. It’s impossible not to be moved by this remarkable endeavour.

title: Pauline died after falling on tram. Her family is still waiting for answers
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaPublic transport Pauline died after falling on tram. Her family is still waiting for answers Gemma Grant October 5, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For Pauline Moore, Melbourne’s tram network connected her to the world. From her home in Hawthorn, the 78-year-old could visit her grandson and buy her own groceries. She could travel to the local library, and make her own way to her regular dialysis appointments at the hospital. Pauline Moore passed away two months after she had a serious fall on a Melbourne tram. But in September 2022, Pauline broke her pelvis during a fall on the tram. Protocol required the immediate evacuation of the tram, and she was forced to call her own ambulance from the footpath, so the tram could be returned to the depot. It left the 78-year-old scared to ride public transport.

Advertisement

Then two months later, Pauline passed away from complications sustained in hospital after the fall. In the four years since her mother’s death, Cath Moore has been asking for greater transparency and accountability from Yarra Trams regarding its safety and first aid policies. Cath Moore’s mother fell on a tram and broke her pelvis. She died two months later following complications in hospital. Chris Hopkins “It’s not good enough … people fall through the cracks, and it’s the most vulnerable members of society who are the ones that should have the most protections afforded them,” Cath said. Between 2016 and 2025, 812 people were injured due to an incident on a Victorian tram, according to statistics from the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator. A further eight passengers died.

Advertisement

Pauline Moore passed away in November 2022, from complications sustained in hospital from a fall on a tram. But deaths like Pauline’s – which happened in the weeks following a fall and included other factors – aren’t necessarily reflected in these statistics. When the 78-year-old boarded a route 48 tram in Richmond, she didn’t have a chance to sit down or hold on before the tram started to move – then brake – and she fell over. The driver carried out a welfare check. Pauline indicated she’d hurt her back, but declined an ambulance at first, partly because she was in shock and disoriented from the fall. As it was a serious incident, Yarra Trams protocol meant that all passengers were unloaded from the tram so it could be sent back to the depot, where it could be inspected for defects and the driver would receive a welfare check.

Advertisement

That left Pauline to call her own ambulance soon after from the footpath. On arrival at the hospital, doctors found she had broken her pelvis. The grandmother was discharged, before later returning to hospital due to a previously undetected second break. During one of these stays, she contracted a bacterial infection – clostridioides difficile – which ultimately led to her death. “She kept saying to me in hospital: ‘If only [the driver] waited another few seconds’ … it haunts me to this day,” Cath said. Cath Moore wants Yarra Trams’ policies to be more accessible and transparent. Chris Hopkins Tram drivers do not need to undertake any first aid training or have medical supplies on board, according to a report by the Public Transport Ombudsman provided to Cath and seen by The Age. Drivers are required to check whether passengers need medical assistance, but aren’t required to call an ambulance if the passenger declines help.

Advertisement

Related Article Public transport Garry was trying to tap on when he fell on a tram. Three weeks later, he was dead Cath said this policy is inherently harmful for older passengers like her mother, who are “conditioned to think that they’re a burden”. “They don’t want to bother. [But] if an old person says ‘No, no, I’m fine,’ you have to use your critical thinking,” she said. A spokesperson from Yarra Trams said that their thoughts remain with Pauline’s family following the tragic incident. They said that after a passenger fall, tram drivers are required to stop and check on the passenger, including asking whether they need help calling an ambulance.

Advertisement

All incidents are also reported by the driver at the end of their shift, the spokesperson said. “Safety of our passengers and people is always our number one priority. We’re constantly working to improve network safety for all passengers, particularly for older and more vulnerable members of the community.” But Cath said Yarra Trams’ protocols remained opaque and not fit-for-purpose. While the ombudsman report indicated that changes had been made to the operator’s First Aid policies following Pauline’s death, the Yarra Trams spokesperson didn’t say what these changes entailed. The spokesperson said that the safety practices across the network are regularly reassessed. Cath would also like to see a more streamlined review process when it comes to victims and their families communicating with organisations like Yarra Trams, the Transport Accident Commission and the ombudsman, which she said are currently siloed.

Advertisement

Related Article Public transport ‘A real kick in the teeth’: Dozens of tram stops have been upgraded, but wheelchair users still can’t board Cath hopes these changes might assist others who are navigating similar heartbreak following an injury or fatality on Melbourne’s network. Ben Rogers, chief executive of the Council on the Ageing (COTA) Victoria and Seniors Rights Victoria, said all public transport needs to constantly strive towards improved accessibility, so the network can best support the state’s older population. “Public transport is a lifeline for many older Victorians. It’s the glue that holds and brings their lives together,” Rogers said. COTA Victoria supports mechanisms like pre-boarding ticket validation, increased on-board announcements and appropriate pauses when a passenger with accessibility needs is boarding or exiting. Similar measures were also recommended by the Victorian Coroners Court in August, after the death of a 78-year-old following a fall on a tram late last year.

Advertisement

Related Article Healthcare Hospital ‘bed block’ fix: How emergency departments are keeping older Victorians at home “[That’s] so we don’t have these unintended falls and consequences that can really impact people’s lives, and in the most horrific form, potentially end it,” Rogers said. Cath Moore said there needs to be tangible changes made, so the process is easier for the family of those involved in incidents to navigate. “I’ve never given up the fight to get mum’s pain recognised by Yarra Trams,” Cath said. “My mother was never interviewed. She was never given an opportunity to tell them what had happened to her … hopefully [policy changes will] save somebody else’s family from the heartache that we’ve gone through.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Children as young as 12 turned away from Perth crisis accommodation

NationalWAHomelessness Children as young as 12 turned away from Perth crisis accommodation Holly Thompson October 5, 2026 — 2:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Crisis accommodation services for at-risk young people across Perth are bursting at the seams, and are being forced to turn away an average of 15 people each day, new data shows. The Ending Child and Youth Homelessness Coalition – a collection of not-for-profits – revealed that between January and June, 19 youth accommodation services across the metropolitan area recorded 2653 occasions where they were unable to provide a young person with a place to stay. Perth is facing a growing crisis, with the CBD a hotspot for young people sleeping rough. Marta Pascual Juanola On average, 69 homeless young people were competing for 1.83 crisis beds in total. A growing proportion of that number are employed. And on August 20 alone, 114 unaccompanied young people – categorised as 25 and under – were recorded as sleeping rough in both Perth and Rockingham.

Advertisement

On Monday, the Coalition released its 2027-28 Pre-Budget Submission, calling on the state government to take the opportunity to get an early start on building a system that “prevents homelessness wherever possible, responds quickly when it happens and helps young people find a safe and stable home”. It developed five actions it would like the government to take, including investing $2 million per year on early intervention, and a further $350,000 to create a dedicated plan to end child and youth homelessness across the state. The Coalition also requested $44.5 million in capital funding and $6.71 million a year to operate new crisis accommodation in Albany and Bayswater, plus $150,000 for a Broome business case and feasibility study. Anonymous stories from those experiencing homelessness were included in the pre-budget submission, with words like dehumanising, alienating, and humiliating being used to describe their experience. One person said that they did not want any more referrals because they could not “deal with the feeling of rejection”.

Advertisement

“I got my hopes up for nothing and left feeling not good enough,” they said. Others described it as “living on the edge”, with every day exhausting to survive through. Sector workers were also included in the pre-budget submission, with one saying they were turning away children as young as 12 and that “youth workers watch them walk away, knowing they face unimaginable dangers alone on the streets.” Another person said they wished they had more power, and that the government would “take us more seriously.” Shelter WA chief executive Kath Snell said they were “pleading with government right now that we don’t see any more of this”.

Advertisement

“We should not be seeing young people and children sleeping rough in a state like WA. We are so incredibly rich, yet we are allowing this to happen,” she said. Another perspective Housing crisis Kristie and Isabel are the faces of WA’s youth homelessness crisis. Here’s what can be done to help them “We have an opportunity now, with this budget coming up, for the government to get on board and support accommodation for those people that are doing it tough, those young people and children that are presenting to services and need help immediately.” A frontline worker from youth homelessness service Passages said: “Day in and day out, our team see young people who have slipped through the cracks, where systems have failed to step in, prevent or intervene early enough in their lives, and now they’re rough sleeping and couch-surfing, often in extremely unsafe and unstable situations.” “It’s also often devastating for our team, especially when we see an unaccompanied child who is particularly vulnerable, knowing that even though we did everything in our power to find them somewhere safe to stay, they’re still going to sleep on the streets that night,” she said.

“We can only hope that when we come back the next day, they are unscathed by that experience. But we know that’s not true. “I think that’s why the sector has higher burnout rates and vicarious trauma – because we see the impact.”
